articles.title: População em situação de rua fica mais tempo presa, aponta CNJ | G1
articles.standfirst: Tempo de encarceramento para desobediência, supera pena máxima para o crime. Estudo conclui que sistema prisional falha em ressocialização por ignorar vulnerabilidades sociais.
articles.summary: Estudo do CNJ revela que a população em situação de rua cumpre penas acima do limite legal no sistema prisional por não ter recursos para o pagamento de multas.
articles.body:
Uma pesquisa do Conselho Nacional de Justiça (CNJ) divulgada nesta quinta-feira (27) aponta que a falta de recursos para o pagamento de multas tem levado a população em situação de rua a permanecer mais tempo presa do que a lei prevê.

Esta é uma das conclusões que consta em um estudo feito sobre população em situação de rua egressa do sistema prisional.

O levantamento aponta que o s crimes mais frequentes imputados à população em situação de rua são:

tráfico de drogas, todos com previsão de aplicação de pena de multa.

No entanto, sem condições financeiras de quitar a sanção, o tempo médio de permanência no sistema prisional aumenta.

A média do tempo de prisão nos casos de desobediência chega a seis anos e meio, quando a pena máxima prevista é de 6 meses.

Para desacato, a média é de quase 2 anos, embora a pena máxima prevista no Código Penal seja de 2 anos. Já para furto, a média do tempo de prisão é de mais de um ano e três meses.

"Medidas penais, como tornozeleira eletrônica, multas, exigências de endereço fixo e obrigações do regime aberto revelam-se frequentemente incompatíveis com a realidade da extrema vulnerabilidade social, produzindo punições por cumprimento impossível", diz o relatório.

A avaliação, feita em parceria com a Pontifícia Universidade Católica de São Paulo (PUC-SP), analisou dados da população carcerária de Porto Alegre (RS), São Paulo (SP), Cuiabá (MT), Salvador (BA), Brasília (DF) e Boa Vista (RR).

O relatório constatou uma subnotificação, diante dos baixos percentuais de pessoas em situação de rua identificadas nos sistemas oficiais.

Do total de 983.564 pessoas com restrição de liberdade no Brasil, apenas 957 foram identificadas como em situação de rua, o que corresponde a 0,10%.

Das pessoas que passaram pelo sistema prisional brasileiro nos últimos cinco anos — 1.107.534 pessoas — apenas 1.168 foram registradas como em situação de rua, um percentual de 0,11%

📍 O estudo apresentou um recorte por capitais:

Em Salvador , das 24.064 pessoas constantes no Sistema Eletrônico de Execução Unificada, apenas 10 foram registradas como em situação de rua (0,04%) e nenhuma pessoa egressa do sistema;

Em Brasília , foram 230 registros entre 108.220 (0,21%) e 45 entre 15.183 pessoas egressas do sistema (0,30%).

Em Cuiabá , 4 registros entre 35.970 pessoas com restrição de liberdade (0,01%) e nenhuma egressa.

Em Boa Vista , 4 registros entre 14.148 pessoas com restrição de liberdade (0,03%) e nenhuma egressa;

Em Porto Alegre , 8 registros entre 42.401 pessoas com restrição de liberdade (0,02%) e nenhuma egressa

"Os números registrados são irrisórios diante da realidade observada em campo, indicando subnotificação maciça e sistemática. Essa lacuna informacional é, em si, o maior obstáculo às análises pretendidas e denota a invisibilidade institucional dessa população".

O Acre apresentou o melhor resultado, com "registros adequados e diligentes", segundo a pesquisa.

Em Rio Branco, 0,93% das pessoas com restrição de liberdade e 2,46% das pessoas egressas são identificadas como em situação de rua, “percentuais muito superiores à média nacional”.

"Isso demonstra que a subnotificação não decorre de problemas técnicos ou tecnológicos dos sistemas, mas sim da falta de adoção das rotinas corretas pelos demais tribunais".

O Tribunal de Justiça de São Paulo (TJSP) passou a alimentar o sistema apenas a partir de outubro de 2025, ao passo que a coleta de dados desta pesquisa foi concluída em janeiro de 2026. O curto período de alimentação inviabilizou a extração de séries históricas consolidadas.

O estudo afirma que a saída do sistema prisional ocorre, em geral, de forma abrupta e desassistida, sem orientação, sem articulação com políticas públicas e sem garantia de condições mínimas de moradia, trabalho ou documentação, o que indica invisibilidade institucional dessa população.

Pessoas em situação de rua no DF. — Foto: TV Globo

A pesquisa conclui que o sistema prisional, especialmente para pessoas em situação de rua, falha em cumprir qualquer função efetiva de ressocialização, produzindo, ao contrário, aprofundamento das vulnerabilidades sociais, rompimento de vínculos e ampliação do estigma.

O estudo defende articulação entre justiça, assistência social, saúde, moradia e trabalho para reconhecer e garantir às pessoas que saem da prisão em situação de rua direitos mínimos e não como objetos permanentes de controle e exclusão.📍

"As entrevistas indicam ainda que as pessoas egressas em situação de rua são atravessadas por um processo persistente de estigmatização social e institucional. Categorias morais, como periculosidade, falta de mérito e desinteresse, orientam práticas institucionais e reforçam a criminalização da pobreza. O estigma atua como uma forma de penalidade prolongada, mantendo barreiras mesmo após o cumprimento da pena".

articles.title: Trump toes line on data centers as more Republicans pump the brakes
articles.summary: Republicans’ growing skepticism of data centers is forcing President Trump to balance his steadfast support for the industry with pushback from his party ahead of the midterm elections. While Trump has doubled down on his support of data centers, the president signaled last week he may give GOP candidates room to oppose the facilities as…
articles.body:
Republicans’ growing skepticism of data centers is forcing President Trump to balance his steadfast support for the industry with pushback from his party ahead of the midterm elections.

While Trump has doubled down on his support of data centers , the president signaled last week he may give GOP candidates room to oppose the facilities as they become a political lightning rod in the midterms.

Trump told reporters last week he wants Republican candidates to “do what they want” on data centers, acknowledging “some people feel differently” on the issue after previously criticizing Democrats for pushing back on planned data center projects.

“If Republicans are against a data center, that’s OK with me,” Trump added. “I’m only saying that if I ran a community … if I was a mayor or if I was a governor in the state, I would want to have the data centers because they bring tremendous income.”

Faced with mounting pressure around the risks of AI and data centers, several high-profile Republicans have abruptly shifted their stance with the midterms just months away.

Those now advocating for stricter restrictions on data centers include not only state leaders such as Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) but also Trump-backed Senate candidates such as Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) and former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.).

“I’d say [Trump’s] been fairly consistent in his messaging. What’s been more malleable is everybody else’s opinion,” one Republican strategist told The Hill.

Mark Weaver, an Ohio-based crisis communications adviser, said he thinks Trump is noticing there is some voter concern about data centers, “and that’s why I think his language has been somewhat muted compared to other things he talks about.”

Still, Weaver thinks Trump will “continue to present a balanced approach of supporting them to ensure that the technology race is not won by China.”

Up until the past few months, the Trump administration framed its light-touch, pro-industry approach to AI as a way to ensure the U.S. remains ahead of China in the so-called AI race.

While competition remains a priority, the administration appeared to tread carefully on its policies as new security risks of AI came into the discussion.

The president’s balancing act was on full display earlier this month when discussing Abbott, a fierce Trump ally, and his shift on data centers

Last November, Abbott called Texas the “epicenter of AI development” as he welcomed Google’s $40 billion investment for the development of data facilities in the Lone Star State.

Now, the governor is arguing data center developers “dug their own grave.” He told ABC’s “This Week” over the weekend that the backlash is what they “deserve” after not collaborating with local governments.

Abbott in June ordered state regulators to audit all data centers seeking to connect to the state’s power grid before project approval. Under the order, project developers are asked for information on whether they are paying their own way or depending on state financial assistance, and on whether they are providing their own power or water to prevent households from bearing the costs.

Amid news of Abbott’s data center initiative, Trump told Punchbowl News that Texas’s approach is a “mistake” while maintaining he is “not taking positions.”

Brendan Steinhauser, a GOP strategist and head of the advocacy group Alliance for Secure AI, said Republicans like Abbott are now seeing “the politics of AI and of data centers specifically kind of turn for the worse.”

“They’ve seen the polling that all of us have seen, but also I think they’re watching what’s happening in the real world,” said Steinhauser, a Texas native.

“They’re seeing a lot of these ‘rogue AI’ loss of control incidents. They’re seeing the Iranians using AI to hack into critical infrastructure, and that’s going to get worse. … They’re seeing the rise of AI companions. The list goes on and on.”

Public concerns around AI quickly increased over the past year, with a recent Pew Research Center poll finding more than half — 52 percent — of surveyed Americans were more concerned than excited about the increased use of AI in daily life, up from 37 percent in 2021.

Data centers are one of the only tangible physical symbols of AI, making them an easy target for overall backlash around AI and its impact on the environment, labor market and utility costs.

Democrats came out hard against the facilitates earlier this year, floating proposals like a national data center moratorium or overhaul of the U.S. tax code to tax AI companies.

Republicans mostly stayed away or echoed Trump, but more are pushing back.

Texas’s Paxton became the latest Republican leader this week to propose restrictions on data centers he would push for if elected to the U.S. Senate this fall. The state prosecutor said his four-point plan will “protect our grid, our communities and our children” while still guaranteeing America beats China in the AI race.

Days earlier, Rogers, who is running in Michigan’s closely watched Senate race, called for a one-year moratorium on data center construction until Michiganders can “get their questions answered” about such projects.

Meanwhile, former Sen. Sherrod Brown (Ohio), the Democratic candidate in Ohio’s Senate race, knocked his opponent, Sen. Jon Husted (R), over the incumbent’s record on data centers in the state. The National Republican Senatorial Committee issued an internal memo last week warning that “data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”

“If he loses and datacenters get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice — and they will not go near the next one,” the memo said.

Steinhauser said he is not surprised by GOP members becoming vocal about the issue, telling The Hill that party members are “willing to have differences of opinion” with Trump on data centers.

“They’re not afraid to say, ‘Well, I don’t agree with him on that,’ or, ‘Yeah, I think this is a mistake.’ I hear it all the time, but they still support him,” Steinhauser said.

Susan Del Percio, a veteran Republican strategist, likened data center outrage to the fracking outrage of the 2010s.

“First communities were welcoming it because it’s so much money, and there really were jobs. … But then people started getting groundwater in their pipes and it started polluting the land,” she said. “A lot of communities who have experienced fracking remember that, so when they see data centers coming in, it makes them nervous.”

So, she said, “it’s a tough needle to thread.”

“Trump never gives in on anything, but I think on this one, there has to be some give somewhere,” she added. “I think you’d rather see Republicans speaking and addressing the concerns on data centers than them talking about how bad tariffs are.”

Multiple Republican strategists agreed there is some level of “risk” for the president to stand behind data centers but also dismissed the notion it would pose as much risk as other issues.

“At the same time, he is the president and he’s responsible for trying to drive policies. … He’s been a pretty strong proponent that having data centers in the country protects the nation and protects the American public in the AI arms race, in particular, against China,” one strategist said under the condition of anonymity to speak freely.

Steinhauser suggested there is a “bit of political risk” for Trump to support the controversial facilities, but it could be more of a risk for potential 2028 Republican presidential nominees such as Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

“They have to navigate this as well, based on what they see on the ground. And obviously, they don’t want to distance themselves from Trump, but they also don’t want to be seen as doing the bidding of Big Tech and the data centers, so they have a really tough situation,” he said.

Still, several strategists have pointed out that it’s a local issue, mostly touching the areas where the data centers are being built or there are plans to build one.

“At this point, the president has to just not publicly attack any Republican who speaks out against the issue,” Del Percio said. “It does not have to be an internal Republican fight unless the president makes it one.”

articles.title: Republicans divided over preelection stimulus push as economy slows
articles.summary: Republicans on Capitol Hill are divided over whether to make a last-ditch push to enact legislation to stimulate the economy and cheer up voters before Election Day as the latest federal data shows the economy is slowing and inflation remains a problem. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) last month floated a fourth budget reconciliation…
articles.body:
Republicans on Capitol Hill are divided over whether to make a last-ditch push to enact legislation to stimulate the economy and cheer up voters before Election Day as the latest federal data shows the economy is slowing and inflation remains a problem.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) last month floated a fourth budget reconciliation package to enact additional progrowth tax cuts. He said the package, which could pass the Senate with a simple majority, would also root out waste and fraud and give more money back to U.S. taxpayers.

Some Senate Republicans have also endorsed the idea of going “big” by using another budget reconciliation bill to boost the economy before potentially losing control of the House or both chambers of Congress in the midterms.

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) has led the charge to provide tariff relief payments to lower- and middle-class Americans struggling to cope with higher cost-of-living expenses amid President Trump’s trade war with Canada and other countries and the slowdown of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

Hawley has introduced legislation to provide $600 tariff rebates to almost all Americans and to their dependent children, which would give $2,400 to a traditional family of four.

The desire to give voters some good news, or at least hope of action on a stimulus package, is driven by indicators showing the economy slowing and polls showing voters largely disapprove of Trump’s handling of the economy.

The Commerce Department on Wednesday reported that the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index rose by 0.2 percent for the month, amounting to an annual inflation rate of 3.7 percent, well above the Federal Reserve’s target of 2 percent.

The data shows that the affordability of goods and services continues to be a major issue.

Economic growth, meanwhile, slowed to 1.5 percent in the second quarter of 2026, cooling down compared with the first quarter of the year, which saw 2.1 percent growth in gross domestic product.

The Conference Board, a nonprofit business membership organization and research group, on Tuesday reported that consumer confidence dropped in August compared with July.

The rising cost of goods and services combined with slowing economic growth has pushed some Republicans in Congress to call for GOP leaders to pursue a more ambitious agenda for the fall.

But that’s getting pushback from other Republican lawmakers who argue that the window to pass additional tax relief or to give families tariff refund payments has closed and that any new economic initiatives won’t pass before the end of the year.

“The rumor is already the House can’t even stay in past one week. They’re going to pass the CR and then skedaddle,” said a Senate GOP aide, referring to talk on Capitol Hill that jittery House Republicans want to get back to the campaign trail as quickly as possible next week after passing a continuing resolution to fund the government until Dec. 11.

“The cake is baked on major policy fights between now and the economy. What are you going to do that would actually change the trajectory of the economy or change any opinions?” said the GOP aide.

The House is scheduled to return to Washington next week to pick up the Senate-passed stopgap measure funding the government until December and then will be on recess again the week of Labor Day.

Both chambers are scheduled to be in session for the final three weeks of September.

Republican Senate and House sources said there hasn’t been much progress on including additional tax relief measures in another budget reconciliation package as Scalise proposed last month.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) has warned against including any instructions to the Senate Finance Committee, which has jurisdiction over tax issues, in a budget resolution, arguing that doing so would open up vulnerable GOP colleagues to tough votes on raising taxes on the wealthy and corporations or extending expired health insurance subsidies.

Thune says forcing vulnerable colleagues such as Sens. Susan Collins (R-Maine), Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) and Jon Husted (R-Ohio) to vote on Democratic amendments designed to score political points would be a “risky proposition.”

Nevertheless, Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) is working on a budget resolution over the August recess in hopes of bringing it to the floor during the September work period to unlock the process to pass a third budget reconciliation package.

The budget framework passed by the House would provide $73 billion in funding for the Pentagon and the nation’s intelligence agencies, $12 billion in aid to farmers and $10 billion to states to tighten rules for voting.

Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas) had argued in June that the reconciliation process should be used to circumvent a Democratic filibuster in the Senate to enact legislation addressing affordability.

Pfluger told the “Ruthless Podcast” in June that the third budget reconciliation bill should address the high costs of housing, energy and other needs.

The third reconciliation package “is us going into our districts, listening to our constituents who are saying, ‘Hey, things are pretty expensive.’ ‘We know it’s not your fault.’ ‘We know it’s Biden and the inflation that he created but what can we do for housing, energy and healthcare?’” he said.

Yet Republican leaders remain strongly opposed to adding tax and healthcare provisions to a budget reconciliation bill that would open up everything under the Finance Committee’s jurisdiction for a debate on the Senate floor.

“You can’t really uncork reconciliation without opening yourself up to a pretty ugly process. You’re going to be revisiting all the Medicaid votes because if you do anything tax-related or tariff-related, you have to instruct Finance, and there’s no desire from a large number of members in the Republican conference to instruct Finance,” said the Senate GOP aide.

articles.title: Trump shifts toward regime change in Iran, but by other means
articles.summary: Team Trump had to find a different pressure point.
articles.body:
The Trump administration is now 181 days into what began as Operation Epic Fury, which later transitioned into a forever ceasefire on day 38.

President Trump has tried unsuccessfully to use the military and diplomatic instruments of national power to bring this war to a conclusion, but a resilient Islamic Republic of Iran has withstood them.

And now he has turned to the economic instrument of national power, in the form of sanctions — supported by a naval blockade on the Strait of Hormuz.

Last Wednesday on Truth Social Trump promised an “Economic D-Day ,” vowing to wield “economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale” against Iran.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent added that Washington expected its allies and rivals to join the ramped-up campaign against Iran. “This is going to be the greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world. And we are going to them and saying you are either with us or against us.”

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi dismissed the threat as a distraction and said it would backfire .

China said U.S. “sanctions and pressure” would not resolve the Iranian war. Foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian said “all relevant parties [need] to take responsible measures and resolve the problem through political and diplomatic means.”

But the White House still does not know who the relevant parties are within the Iranian regime. They tried Araghchi and the Speaker of Iran’s parliament, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf. They even tried backdoor negotiations with Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps commander Maj. Gen. Ahmad Vahidi.

But is Trump’s Economic D-Day just regime change repackaged?

Since the onset of Operations Epic Fury and Roaring Lion, the goal has been regime change. Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have said as much — Trump during his Feb. 28 speech to the American public, and Netanyahu on March 13.

The plan was to set conditions for the Iranian people to rise up and “take back their country.” Removing the Supreme Leader and his senior advisors on day one did not have that effect. Although Iran’s conventional military was decimated, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps — the regime’s center of gravity — was still in place, along with its Basij paramilitary , whose mission is to keep the Iranian people under control. And they did.

At day 38, Trump abandoned his military campaign to negotiate with what was left of the regime. But the new faces that emerged carried the same torch. Thus began the forever cease-fire and pursuit of a deal.

A 14-point memorandum of understanding and a 60-day cease-fire eventually emerged. Neither lasted, in large part because Iran’s negotiators and the people actually in charge were not on the same sheet of music .

The hard-liners were not going to give up the Strait of Hormuz, nor their enriched uranium nor the pursuit of a nuclear weapon. They were intent on shutting down the strait — their only leverage. Tit-for-tat military responses prevailed.

The regime never felt threatened by the Trump administration. The welfare of their citizens was not their concern — only their regime’s survival.

Having reached this impasse, team Trump had to find a different pressure point. But Trump himself was hesitant. Those words of caution Gen. Colin Powell provided President George W. Bush in August 2002 during the run up to Operation Iraqi Freedom were playing in Trump’s head: “If you take out a government, take out a regime, guess who becomes the government and regime and is responsible for the country? You are. So if you break it, you own it.”

Trump saw what happened in Iraq and later in Afghanistan — and he wants no part of nation-building in Iran. He would rather make a deal with the current regime than remove it.

But maybe he would not have to — maybe the Iranian people could do it for him.

In January 2026, a nationwide uprising took place in Iran as economic protests in the Grand Bazaar in Tehran expanded to more than 400 locations nationwide. Merchants and citizens took to the streets in anti-government demonstrations calling for an end to the Islamic Republic.

The main reason the protests began in the Bazaar was the severe economic crisis and the collapse of the Iranian currency. In late December 2025, the Iranian rial had fallen to its lowest historical level against the U.S. dollar, placing immense pressure on the public and merchants struggling to price their goods.

Security forces executed a brutal and unprecedented crackdown on the protesters, along with implementing a near-total internet blackout, killing as many as 36,500 civilians and arresting over 1,500 .

Monday afternoon Bessent delivered the message, Operation Economic Outcast had begun.

The rial had already dropped to 2.02 million to the U.S. dollar when trading opened earlier that morning. By recreating deplorable economic conditions in Iran similar to those in January 2026, is the intent to incite an uprising to overthrow the regime?

Setting conditions is one thing — having a plan to support and then exploit those conditions is another. Instruments of national power work best when used together. Has the White House learned that lesson?

Col. (Ret.) Jonathan Sweet served 30 years as a military intelligence officer and led the U.S. European Command Intelligence Engagement Division from 2012 to 2014. Mark Toth writes on national security and foreign policy. They are the cofounders of INTREP360 and the INTREP360 Intelligence Report on Substack.

articles.title: On the Ballot: Markey-Moulton match-up underlines competing visions for change in Democratic Party
articles.summary: Rep. Seth Moulton and Sen. Ed Markey are squaring off for Massachusetts’s Democratic Senate nod next week in the latest primary to spotlight young challengers vying to push out the party’s old guard. Moulton, a 47-year-old who’s been in the House for six terms, is mounting a long-shot bid to unseat Markey, who at 80 has served on Capitol Hill for…
articles.body:
Rep. Seth Moulton and Sen. Ed Markey are squaring off for Massachusetts’s Democratic Senate nod next week in the latest primary to spotlight young challengers vying to push out the party’s old guard.

Moulton, a 47-year-old who’s been in the House for six terms, is mounting a long-shot bid to unseat Markey, who at 80 has served on Capitol Hill for five decades, including 20 terms in the House.

The younger challenger has framed the race around generational change and questioned Markey’s progressive bona fides, while the incumbent has touted his long record in Congress, his progressive ethos and support from juggernauts like Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.).

The campaigns offer dueling visions of “what constitutes change,” according to Jesse Rhodes , a political science professor at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and co-director of the UMass Poll.

“There’s the symbolism around age and a shift to a new generation, and that is, for Moulton and his supporters, the key dimension of change that they envision,” Rhodes added.

“But I think Markey and his supporters have countered with the argument that what really is needed is a vigorous progressive Democratic Party,” he continued.

Markey maintains the edge in polling ahead of Tuesday’s primary, but momentum has nevertheless built around Moulton in what’s one of this primary season’s last major tests of Democratic appetite for younger Senate hopefuls.

Moulton has made the generational conversation a key part of his campaign since launching his challenge last year — in a cycle marked by the passing of multiple Capitol Hill Democrats in office, renewed talk of age and term limits , as well as the fallout from former President Biden’s decision to end his 2024 campaign amid age and health concerns .

“I’m running against the senator’s decision after 50 years in Washington, to run for another term at age 80,” the congressman said in a final debate last week, where he voiced support for age limits in Congress. “I believe in a new generation of leadership. I believe we can do better than the status quo.”

The Boston Globe endorsed Moulton over Markey last week, suggesting that the younger candidate “can bring new vision and vigor to an aging, ailing, and deeply unpopular Democratic Party.”

Markey, though, argued at the recent debate that it’s Moulton who has had “a hard time keeping up” with the incumbent on the campaign trail, pledging that he’s “more energized than ever before.”

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) backed Markey last week, lauding the incumbent’s record.

The primary is one of several this cycle in which younger challengers have taken aim at longtime lawmakers. But in many of the races, the challengers were also running clearly to the left of the incumbents.

Democratic Reps. Diana DeGette (Colo.), Shri Thanedar (Mich.) and Adriano Espaillat (N.Y.) — aged 69, 71 and 71, respectively — all lost to younger challengers backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). Colorado’s Melat Kiros , Michigan’s Donavan McKinney and New York’s Darializa Avila Chevalie r are 29, 34 and 32, respectively.

In the Massachusetts race, it’s the longtime incumbent who’s rallied progressive support, while his challenger is seen as more moderate.

“The Markey-Moulton primary is a little bit of an outlier, because the positions are kind of reversed in interesting ways: that the challenger Moulton is younger, but he’s also more moderate,” said Rhodes.

But Jennifer Holdsworth , a former Moulton adviser and Democratic strategist, pushed back against the popular framing of the race, calling it “unfortunate tribalism” and arguing that Moulton has called for a number of “very progressive” platforms.

“It’s not easy to place him in an ideological clan of the party, and I think that’s actually what voters are looking for moving forward. They’re tired of the left, right, center debate. Voters themselves don’t see themselves that way,” Holdsworth said of Moulton.

“It really is a question about whether someone in their 80s is simply too old to weigh in on the biggest policy debates of our time,” she added, pointing to the rivals’ debate stage clash over AI last week.

With just days to go before the Markey-Moulton showdown, UMass polling last week found the incumbent was backed by more than 4 in 5 likely Democratic primary voters, signaling that Markey’s age “may actually be advantageous” to the incumbent as voters labeled him progressive, experienced and trustworthy.

“In general, we just need to be attentive to, I think, two interrelated but distinct battles in the Democratic Party. One is about incumbency and ossification and just getting too cozy in office, but the other is about the kind of ideological soul of the Democratic Party and where it’s going to go,” Rhodes said.

He pointed to Sanders, who at 84 is the second-oldest senator, behind only 92-year-old Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa). He’s served in the Senate for 20 years and will finish his current term in 2031, at age 89 — but as one of the leading progressives on Capitol Hill, he hasn’t faced significant calls to step aside.

“Is Bernie an example of the past that needs to go, or is he a forerunner of the future where the Democratic Party is going to be leaning in as we go forward?” Rhodes said.

Another unique contour in the race is that, while Markey has served in Washington for 50 years, Moulton has already put in a decade in the House.

“While undoubtedly experience matters, the question is: what kind of experience?” Holdsworth said.

Regardless, Markey remains in a strong position to retain his Senate seat for another six-year term. He faced a strong challenge from former Rep. Joe Kennedy III (D-Mass.) in 2020 but defeated his rival by roughly 10 percentage points in the primary, marking the first time a Kennedy family member lost a statewide race in Massachusetts.

The marquee Senate race is not the only race in the Bay State with age on the ballot. Thirty-nine-year-old lawyer Patrick Roath , backed by David Hogg’s Leaders We Deserve, is challenging 71-year-old Rep. Stephen Lynch (D-Mass.) in the Democratic primary for Massachussett’s safely blue 8th Congressional District.

Roath has centered the race around change, while hammering Lynch over past votes against former President Obama’s signature healthcare policy in 2010 and in support of the Laken Riley Act last year.

Democrats see the Lynch-Roath primary as more emblematic of the broader themes bedeviling the party of age and generational change.

“That race is a wild card race,” one Massachusetts Democratic strategist supporting Markey in the Senate primary told The Hill regarding Lynch’s reelection.

“Roath is challenging Stephen from the left,” the strategist said, adding that “Moulton is really challenging Markey from the right.”

Roath told The Hill in a statement that Democrats “are looking for outsider candidates challenging the status quo.”

Lynch, however, has touted his experience, the amount of money he’s directed toward his district and pointed to legislation like the DREAM Act that he’s supported while in office.

“And remember, I accomplished much of that as a member of the minority party in Congress,” Lynch said during opening statements at a candidate forum this month. “You can only imagine what we can do together if the situation changes.”

A second Massachusetts Democratic strategist who has previously worked for Moulton, but is not involved in either the Senate or House race, suggested Roath could have a shot at ousting Lynch.

“I think the looming question for Moulton and Roath is have they deemed themselves acceptable alternatives to the incumbent?” the second strategist added. “And that’s a challenge in any primary.”

Welcome to The Hill’s On The Ballot. We’re Julia Mueller and Caroline Vakil — reach out to us on X ( @jmthewriter + @CarolineVakil) or via email ( jmueller@thehill.com + cvakil@thehill.com.)

The 2028 shadow primaries are on display in key states. And these potential candidates want you to know they’re traveling.

Does the early bird catch the worm? A handful of Democrats and even some Republicans are testing that idiom out in real-time as they flock to Iowa, New Hampshire and South Carolina.

Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg headlined an Iowa Democratic Party event in July and traveled to Reno earlier this month to campaign alongside several candidates. He swung through South Carolina this month, too, attending a state party conference in Florence and making an appearance at Claflin University, a historically Black university (HBCU), in Orangeburg.

Those Palmetto State stops prompted a curt reply from Izzy Gardon, a spokesman for another likely 2028er, California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), who replied to a post of Buttigieg attending an NAACP event, writing on the social platform X, “First time in SC in 3 years? Nice!”

It’s a prickly issue, particularly because Buttigieg dropped his presidential campaign in 2020 after placing fourth in the South Carolina Democratic contest. Buttigieg notably won the Iowa caucuses that year and placed second in New Hampshire. South Carolina will be the first state to vote in the Democratic primary in 2028.

Newsom, too, has attracted attention for a tour through Michigan , which is also part of Democrats’ early roster of presidential primary states. He posted about visiting Fellowship Chapel in Detroit and campaigned alongside Michigan legislative candidates as Democrats look to flip back the state House this fall.

Though the California governor caught some flack for not meeting with a pair of Michigan’s key power players, like Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) and Democratic National Committee (DNC) Black Caucus chair Virgie Rollins, Politico reported .

Newsom, of course, is no stranger to the early states. He did a multi-county swing through South Carolina last year and stopped in the Granite State earlier this year to promote his memoir, “Young Man in a Hurry.”

Republicans also haven’t been shy to show off their recent travels. Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), a potential 2028 candidate, made an appearance in the Hawkeye State in May for an event and campaigned for Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird last month.

Cruz is one of the most prominent likely 2028ers to weigh in on GOP primaries this year, even if it’s meant putting himself at odds with President Trump .

U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth also attended events at the Iowa State Fair earlier this month alongside Bird and Rep. Zach Nunn (R-Iowa), respectively. Blanche told NBC News in a recent interview that he was not running for president. The Pentagon made clear that Hegseth was traveling to Iowa in his “personal capacity.”

Republicans’ growing skepticism over data centers is forcing President Trump to balance his steadfast support for the industry as party candidates reckon with constituents’ concerns over the AI infrastructure, The Hill’s Miranda Nazarro and Mallory Wilson report.

A federal judge in Boston on Wednesday lifted a nationwide block on mail-in voting restrictions, temporarily clearing the way for the Trump administration to begin implementing them ahead of the November midterms. Read more from The Hill’s Sophie Brams.

Democrat David Crowley and Republican Tom Tiffany are tied in a new poll of the Wisconsin gubernatorial race, suggesting a tight race in the presidential swing state, The Hill’s Tara Suter reports.

As the midterm cycle heats up, we’re asking folks in the elections space what they’re consuming on and off the campaign trail. Sophia Vento is The Hill’s campaign editor.

A Minnesota native, she attended the University of Wisconsin-Madison and now lives in Washington, D.C. Sophia edits this very newsletter.

I’m currently reading “The Colony” by Annika Norlin. It’s about a burnt-out journalist (lol) that encounters a commune of sorts in the Swedish forest. I’m about halfway through the novel, and it’s gripping. I don’t want to give too much away, but you learn how each member of the mysterious group came to reside in the isolated countryside.

I also recently finished reading “Famesick” by Lena Dunham and “The Night of the Gun” by David Carr. I love a memoir.

On a typical day in the office, you can find me snacking on carrots and peppers with hummus. On election nights, I’m indulging in any and all sour candy.

What album or podcast do you have on repeat?

I’m usually listening to music at the gym or on a run, so it’s a lot of pop — Charli XCX, Lorde, Harry Styles. Bad Bunny of course. I also am a pretty regular listener of the podcast “How Long Gone.” It scratches a gossipy itch.

In the morning, coffee with honey and a splash of half-and-half. Usually hot, preferably iced. Diet Coke as a treat on occasion.

What TV show are you watching right now?

I’m always watching whichever “Real Housewives” franchise is airing. I’m patiently waiting for “Real Housewives of Salt Lake City” to start in September. I’ve also been re-watching “Veep,” which has been cathartic yet slightly triggering.

What are your favorite restaurants in Minnesota (and Wisconsin)?

I have too many thoughts and opinions to share on this topic. When I’m back home in Minnesota, I’m always picking up dinner from Nong’s Thai Cuisine in my hometown (shout out to Golden Valley). I also love The Monte Carlo in Minneapolis — particularly the martinis, chicken wings and green beans (trust me).

It would be criminal to not mention the Minnesota State Fair (which runs from Aug. 27 to Sept. 7). It’s the happiest place on Earth. Get the deep-fried Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups from Deep Fried Candy Bars, a burger from the Midway Mens Club and garlic fries from Ball Park Cafe.

articles.title: Florida becomes first state to block welfare cash for tattoos, vapes and more
articles.summary: Florida will bar welfare benefits from covering tattoos, theme-park tickets, video games, vapes and other nonessential purchases under a first-in-the-nation plan Trump wants other states to follow.
articles.body: Florida is becoming the first state to impose sweeping new limits on how welfare cash can be spent, blocking recipients from using cash-assistance benefits loaded onto EBT cards for purchases like tattoos, theme park tickets, video games, vaping products and other items not generally considered "basic needs" under a plan the Trump administration is urging other states to emulate. Florida’s cash-assistance program, known as Temporary Cash Assistance (TCA), is funded through the federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) program. It is separate from SNAP, the food-assistance program, though families may receive both types of benefits through separate balances on the same EBT card. The Department of Health and Human Services' Administration for Children and Families (ACF) determined Florida’s updated TANF plan to be complete Thursday in a letter sent to Gov. Ron DeSantis and obtained by Fox News Digital. The letter praised the Sunshine State governor for putting "common-sense restrictions" on what it calls inappropriate, luxury and non-essential purchases. MICHIGAN LAWMAKER MOVES TO SHUT DOWN 'GUARDRAIL-FREE' CASH HANDOUT PROGRAM FOR NEW MOTHERS "Taxpayer-funded assistance should help families put food on the table, keep the lights on, purchase clothing, provide for their children and overcome barriers on the path toward independence," DeSantis said in announcing the policy. "We will continue supporting Floridians who genuinely need assistance, while working to improve accountability and transparency so that these programs operate as intended." Florida had already barred EBT cards from being used or accepted for alcohol purchases and transactions at adult-entertainment establishments, casinos and commercial bingo locations several years ago, but the updated plan moves beyond those merchant and location-based restrictions by imposing item-level limits at otherwise eligible retailers, including on purchases for tattoos and other body piercings, entertainment services and products like theme park admission and video games, intoxicants like vapes and other nicotine products, and pornography products. SEE IT: SNAP ADVOCATE DEFENDS TAXPAYER-FUNDED COCA-COLA IN FIERY EXCHANGE WITH GOP LAWMAKER ON WASTE The governor's press release announcing the change also cites "Psychic and fortune-telling services" among those purchases that will be prohibited. Florida’s separate Healthy SNAP initiative, launched in April, barred recipients from using food benefits on soda, energy drinks, candy and ultra-processed prepared desserts. The new action from the Sunshine State, with backing from the Trump administration, applies those same food limits to Florida’s cash-assistance program, which is funded through TANF, while adding restrictions on non-food purchases deemed non-essential. FOOD STAMP FRAUD CRACKDOWN AT USDA WOULD END LOOPHOLE THAT LETS FERRARI, LAMBORGHINI OWNERS GET BENEFITS ACF Assistant Secretary Alex J. Adams told Fox News Digital the administration sees TANF as temporary help for families in need, not an unrestricted cash benefit. "When people come to us for those basic needs, we will give them short-term assistance for those needs, but not for superfluous purchases," he said. FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE WELFARE FRAUD AS COMMON, STILL MOSTLY FAVOR PROTECTING BENEFITS OVER CRACKDOWNS Florida distributes its welfare benefits through EBT cards to help eligible families cover basics such as food, clothing, housing, utilities, household goods and personal-care items. The governor’s office says the average participating household receives roughly $250 a month, and Adams stressed that the policy does not reduce anyone’s benefit amount. "No one loses any of their benefit," Adams said. "What this is saying is, if an individual or a family is going to come to the government to cover their basic needs, it is the government’s expectation that they be used for those basic needs." The restrictions will be phased in as Florida works with its EBT vendor and participating retailers to block prohibited purchases. Under the final plan, recipients will be allowed to withdraw TCA cash only at SNAP-authorized retailers and financial institutions that accept EBT cards. Adams told Fox News Digital the administration hopes Florida becomes a model for other states. He said 27 states lack EBT location restrictions beyond those required by federal law and that most states do not impose item-level TANF purchase limits. articles.title: House Democrat pushes back on ‘nutty stuff’ some in DSA support
articles.summary: Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-Md.) on Wednesday pushed back on some of the policy proposals included in the Democratic Socialists of America’s (DSA) platform, calling it “nutty stuff.” Ivey said in an interview with NewsNation’s Blake Burman on “The Hill” that he thinks it will be “interesting” to see “what part of DSA these guys actually…
articles.body:
Rep. Glenn Ivey (D-Md.) on Wednesday pushed back on some of the policy proposals included in the Democratic Socialists of America’s (DSA) platform, calling it “nutty stuff.”

Ivey said in an interview with NewsNation’s Blake Burman on “The Hill” that he thinks it will be “interesting” to see “what part of DSA these guys actually are.” He later added that there is “the other part of it out there, too.”

“I saw the president of the DSA talking about, you know, eliminating prisons and, you know, eliminating the Senate,” he said. “And I just think that’s kind of nutty stuff that, you know, really, I’m not going to support. And I don’t think any voters anywhere will.”

He said that new DSA-aligned members of Congress should go to Washington to see what “they stand for and what they want to do” while working within the Democratic caucus.

“I think that they’re, you know, people, especially those who’ve already been state legislators, they sound like they’re, you know, focused on affordability, making sure that we can help people, you know, put food on the table, you know, pay for ga, get health care coverage, the things that House Democrats are already focused on,” Ivey told Burman.

Burman asked Ivey about the issues DSA members campaign on, to which Ivey said that he only saw the resurfaced remarks from former Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong (D) calling to “ cancel Thanksgiving ,” which she later walked back . Ivey said this issue was the “craziest” he had seen.

“The ones that I’ve seen so far are on the affordability message and focus on the things that voters really care about,” Ivey added.

Democratic candidates aligned with DSA have led a rising tide of primary victories against many more moderate, establishment Democrats. The victories have laid bare the divisions within the Democratic Party, particularly over issues like the cost of living and U.S. support for Israel, but some incumbents have argued that their party’s “big tent” allows for a diversity of opinions.

Some lawmakers, including Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), have not dismissed the DSA’s impact in supporting candidates, though he said he “ certainly isn’t seeking ” their endorsement.

But Democrats who have warded off DSA challenges have pushed back against the “big tent” narrative, including Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.), who won his recent primary against Oliver Larkin earlier this month.

Moskowitz told Fox Business Network that Democrats will have to see if new DSA-aligned members can “coexist” with them, but “they can’t coexist with me .”

Candidates affiliated with the left-wing organization have won primaries in states like New York , Florida and Pennsylvania , with some advancing to runoff races in cities like Washington, D.C., and Los Angeles . Other candidates like Hong and Larkin failed to win votes at the polls.

articles.title: South Carolina Senate Democratic nominee: ‘Medicare for All is a policy from a few decades ago’
articles.summary: South Carolina Senate Democratic nominee Annie Andrews on Wednesday dismissed “Medicare for All” as an outdated policy as she seeks to become the first Democrat to win a statewide race in the Palmetto State in more than 25 years. “Medicare for All is a policy from a few decades ago,” Andrews, a physician, told host…
articles.body:
South Carolina Senate Democratic nominee Annie Andrews on Wednesday dismissed “Medicare for All” as an outdated policy as she seeks to become the first Democrat to win a statewide race in the Palmetto State in more than 25 years.

“Medicare for All is a policy from a few decades ago,” Andrews, a physician, told host Leland Vittert on NewsNation’s “On Balance.”

She added, “I’m a pragmatic person. When you work as a physician, you have to be a problem solver. You roll up your sleeves, you solve the problem in front of you, you work with whoever you need to work with, you don’t let perfect be the enemy of good.”

Andrews is facing off against Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), who defeated Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) in Tuesday’s GOP runoff to take the spot of her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), on the ballot.

As of Tuesday, Decision Desk HQ gave Darline Graham an 81 percent chance to beat Andrews in the general election. A Democrat has not won a statewide election in South Carolina since former Sen. Fritz Hollings (D-S.C.) and former Gov. Jim Hodges (D) did so in 1998.

In reliably conservative South Carolina, Andrews has campaigned as a moderate, including on healthcare.

“I believe with every cell in my body that healthcare is a human right,” she told Vittert. “But I’m also a realist, and I understand where we are politically in this country right now. We have to take pragmatic solutions to fix our healthcare system, shift it from a profit-motivated system to a patient-centered system.”

Thirty-five percent of respondents to a survey the Pew Research Center conducted last November preferred a single government-run health insurance system , while 31 percent said private companies and the government should offer insurance.

Progressive lawmakers and candidates have made Medicare for All their signature domestic policy proposal, after Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) staunchly advocated for such a system during his two unsuccessful presidential campaigns.

The Medicare for All Act, introduced by Sanders and Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) last year, has 17 co-sponsors in the Senate and 114 in the House .

But Andrews said Wednesday the “next step” lawmakers should take is tacking on a public option to the Affordable Care Act (ACA) and halting Medicaid cuts the Trump administration made under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

The Democratic nominee also argued for “reinstituting” the ACA premium subsidies that expired at the end of last year and “fully funding” the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and National Institutes of Health.

“At some point, we’ll be able to have a productive bipartisan conversation about how we actually build a healthcare system that meets the needs of every American,” Andrews noted.

articles.title: Karoline Leavitt reveals she’s advised Trump on White House replacement in final interview as press secretary
articles.summary: Karoline Leavitt says she has been privately advising Trump on her successor as White House press secretary candidates line up for the role.
articles.body: Karoline Leavitt may be stepping away from the White House podium, but she still has the president's ear on who takes her place. In her final official interview as White House press secretary Thursday, Leavitt revealed she has been privately advising President Donald Trump on her successor as candidates line up for the high-profile role. "Of course, we've spoken about it," Leavitt told "Fox & Friends." KAROLINE LEAVITT REVEALS NEXT ROLE AFTER LEAVING WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY POST "One thing I'll say is there is no shortage of applications. There's a lot of people who want this job, a lot of capable people who want this job," she added. Leavitt did not name any contenders but said she has given Trump her advice on the qualities his next press secretary should possess and hopes to remain involved until he makes his decision. WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENTS WIDELY PRAISE KAROLINE LEAVITT AS SHE ANNOUNCES EXIT FROM TRUMP ADMINISTRATION After nearly 20 months as Trump's primary public-facing messenger, Leavitt said there is one requirement she believes is indispensable: the president's complete trust. "Ultimately, it has to be his decision to make. [The] press secretary and the president – you spend a lot of time together – it has to be someone he trusts fully, and I know he'll make the right decision at the right time, and I'll be here to help him if he continues to want me to do so," she said. Leavitt also reflected on her time in the role, calling her departure "bittersweet" as she prepares to step back from the White House to spend more time with her two young children. There will never be another like him and to serve as his spokesperson behind that podium. It has been the adventure of a lifetime," she added. Leavitt said Trump's support extended beyond giving her the job, describing him as an understanding "boss and a friend" as she made the decision to leave the West Wing.

articles.title: House Intel Chair: ‘Joint service environment’ needs to prepare for future conflicts
articles.summary: House Intelligence Committee Chair Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) on Wednesday said the intelligence community needs to buy into a “joint service environment” in which the lines of communication are open and fluid. He referenced the joint effort after the 9/11 terrorist attacks as a similar environment officials should be operating under as the U.S. tracks drone…
articles.body:
House Intelligence Committee Chair Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) on Wednesday said the intelligence community needs to buy into a “joint service environment” in which the lines of communication are open and fluid.

He referenced the joint effort after the 9/11 terrorist attacks as a similar environment officials should be operating under as the U.S. tracks drone threats and other dangers globally.

“The whole 9/11 Commission said we suffered from a failure of imagination. We now have AI and drone warfare. We’re behind the eight ball a bit, according to many military experts, when it comes to drones. AI is like the big unknown right now,” Crawford said Wednesday on NewsNation’s “Elizabeth Vargas Reports.”

“We don’t know what we’re unleashing as we create it,” he added.

In reference to drone threats, Crawford says the U.S. can spur better military readiness by communicating frequently.

“I think what this calls for is recognizing what we did right, and what we did right was to sort of break down the walls that were preventing our agencies from communicating,” he said of conditions after the terrorist attacks on Sept. 11, 2001.

“So there are some things we need to do further with that. We need to foster a joint service environment, a culture in the IC, the intelligence community, that understands, much like the military, the military was better because they recognized the need to work together because not one single branch can do it all,” he added.

The leadership of the U.S. national security policy remains in flux after a Signal scandal last year resulted in reassignment of former national security adviser Mike Waltz.

Waltz now serves as an ambassador to NATO, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio serves in the interim as national security adviser.

Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard also resigned in June to help take care of her husband, who was diagnosed with cancer.

Former U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York Jay Clayton took Gabbard’s place this month after being approved by the Senate in a 51-47 vote.

In June, reports emerged that the CIA stopped sharing information with the Office of National Intelligence following a dispute over their responsibilities under Gabbard’s leadership.

articles.title: Leavitt talks about what’s next for her on last day at White House
articles.summary: White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said there’s “definitely a list” of who could be her successor but that no decisions have been made yet as she takes on her last day in the role. “As for who the president chooses next, it is a decision that is entirely up to him,” Leavitt said Thursday…
articles.body:
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said there’s “definitely a list” of who could be her successor but that no decisions have been made yet as she takes on her last day in the role.

“As for who the president chooses next, it is a decision that is entirely up to him,” Leavitt said Thursday in an appearance on NewsNation , The Hill’s sister network.

“Obviously whoever takes this job, you spend a lot of time with the president, has to be someone he wholeheartedly trusts and believes in,” she added.

The outgoing press secretary explained that she’s offered up her “advice and counsel” on whom President Trump should pick next.

“It is a blessing, a privilege and honor to stand behind the White House podium,” she said. “So, whoever gets the job next is a very lucky person to work for this president at this moment in history, and I’ll be here to help every step of the way.”

Leavitt also noted she would still be working as an outside adviser. She confirmed last week that she is set to work at Trump’s MAGA Inc. super PAC . She didn’t share what her title would be.

When announcing her departure, Trump said Leavitt will be “an influential voice within the Republican Party” ahead of the midterms.

She told NewsNation that she has learned “so much” from Trump on how to handle the media.

“I mean, he was, of course, a businessman, built a business empire in New York City and was on the front pages of many tabloids and was spinning up the press before I was even alive,” Leavitt continued. “He’s a pro.”

She added that she is “grateful to the president for being so understanding of me and my family in this very difficult decision.”

Leavitt gave birth to her first child in July 2024 while serving on the president’s reelection campaign. She had to quickly return to her post after the attempted assassination on Trump’s life at a rally in Butler, Pa., just three days after she had her son.

She had her second child in May. She held her first briefing after maternity leave on July 16 and earlier this month announced she was leaving the position.

“Every day as a working mother is a challenge,” the departing press secretary said. “You have to make sacrifices. You have to prioritize your time, and you have to say no to a lot of opportunities that come your way because you want to be there for bedtime with your kids every night.”

“I think the birth of my daughter … really just showed me that, you know, two children at home who deserve and need their mother’s constant attention and presence,” she added.

Leavitt spent 20 months in the role, and her departure marks the end of the tenure of the youngest White House press secretary in history, as she took the role at 27 years old.

She called it “the honor and blessing of my life to serve as his spokesperson,” adding that Trump was the “best boss.”

“It has been the adventure of a lifetime,” Leavitt said.

articles.title: To match Denmark’s public health, we need more than its vaccine model
articles.summary: There are plenty of lessons the U.S. should take from countries such as Denmark, but vaccine policy is not one of them.
articles.body:
On Aug. 10, President Trump signed an executive order calling for the U.S. to follow a significantly reduced childhood vaccine schedule. Trump said the change would “finally align the United States with other advanced and developed nations around the world.”

This move will not only endanger American families but also push the nation’s already poor health outcomes further behind our global peers. There are plenty of lessons the U.S. should take from countries such as Denmark, but vaccine policy is not one of them.

I have spent my career studying healthcare systems, in the U.S. and across the globe. I agree with the premise that America should look abroad for lessons about how to improve our health. Americans spend more on healthcare than anyone else in the world, yet we live shorter lives and are less healthy than people in many countries that spend far less.

Denmark, Germany and Japan are excellent places to find a better roadmap. They consistently outperform the U.S. on many measures of health — their residents live longer, have healthier babies and suffer far less from chronic illness. But this is not because they have different vaccine schedules. In fact, the U.S. vaccine schedule is closely aligned with many peer nations. The diseases we target, the vaccines we use and the timing are largely similar.

Denmark is actually something of an outlier. Its schedule reflects choices made for a relatively small, homogeneous country with universal care and low baseline disease rates — conditions that don’t apply in the U.S. And countries with stronger primary care systems can often achieve the same levels of protection with fewer doses because they are better able to ensure children receive care on time. The U.S. builds in more doses primarily as a buffer against a more fragmented system.

That is the problem with looking at Denmark’s vaccine schedule in isolation. If we want to understand why people in Denmark and other peer countries are healthier, we should be asking the following questions: Why do people in these countries have better access to care, stronger health outcomes and longer lifespans? How did they build affordable, accessible healthcare systems that treat people before they get sick?

The answers, it turns out, are not that complicated.

Denmark, Germany, Japan and many other countries have invested in health systems that offer universal health coverage and affordable care. People in these countries generally have access to a regular primary care doctor and can get an appointment when they need one. Their prescription drugs are far more affordable, and vaccines are free and widely available. Mothers and children receive stronger support through the healthcare system and through public health policies that help families meet basic needs.

Because of these sustained healthcare investments, diseases are diagnosed earlier, chronic conditions are managed more effectively, preventive care is stronger and mothers, infants and children are healthier.

Denmark , which the Make America Healthy Again movement often singles out as a health success story, is a case in point. Its excellent outcomes did not emerge from a single policy or a particular vaccine schedule. They are the result of decades of wise policy choices aimed at building a healthcare system that routinely delivers accessible, affordable quality care.

Today, millions of Americans remain uninsured or underinsured. Many more have coverage but still face high deductibles and out-of-pocket costs, forcing millions to delay doctor-recommended care. The price of prescription drugs forces some patients to skip medications or ration doses. We consistently experience higher rates of preventable illness and mortality. All the while, medical debt remains a daily reality for families across the U.S. Again and again, we spend more and get less.

If we truly want to make America healthy again, we should start with the policies that make other countries healthy. That means making healthcare and prescription drugs more accessible and affordable. It means investing in primary care, maternal and child health, prevention and public health. It means building a system that promotes health throughout life rather than one that too often waits until illness becomes a crisis.

It is smart to look abroad to improve America’s health. There is a lot we can learn from Denmark, Germany and Japan, but the biggest lesson isn’t found in their vaccine schedules. It is found in the health security enjoyed by all their residents. Health is built by investments and policies that ensure care is not an exclusive privilege but a fundamental right for all.

Reginald D. Williams II is senior vice president and leader of the international health program at the Commonwealth Fund.

articles.body:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer accused of shooting a Venezuelan man in the leg during an immigration crackdown in Minnesota earlier this year was released from a Texas jail on Thursday morning, a day after a judge declined to force his extradition.

Christian Castro was freed from custody just before 7 a.m. local time, Cameron County Sheriff Manuel Treviño confirmed in an email to The Hill.

Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz (D) sued Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) last week after alleging Abbott had refused to sign the paperwork authorizing Castro’s transfer so he could face charges in connection with the January shooting.

Castro had remained behind bars since his arrest in late May but legally could not be held longer than 90 days while awaiting extradition.

U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. ruled Wednesday that Minnesota’s bid was not ripe for consideration because no final action had been taken yet.

“Minnesota alleges that Governor Abbott has ‘refused to sign’ and has ‘with[eld]’ the rendition warrant. But the record reflects only that Governor Abbott has neither agreed nor refused to sign the rendition warrant as to Castro,” Rodriguez wrote.

Abbott argued that he was not obligated to hand Castro over to Minnesota authorities while the Texas secretary of state’s office reviews whether Castro meets the definition of a “fugitive” under federal extradition law.

Minnesota was also pushing to keep Castro in custody, warning that he may try to flee the country once released. Court filings show that the state raised concerns about repeated jailhouse phone calls between the officer and a woman who lives in Mexico, during which he “expressed a desire to purchase property” in the country and “move there in the future.”

“Minnesota should never have had to file this lawsuit or this motion,” Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison (D) said in a Wednesday statement. “Greg Abbott has a black-letter legal and constitutional duty to sign the rendition warrant to return the fugitive Castro to Minnesota — full stop — and we are only here because Abbott is playing with constitutional fire.”

Castro is facing four counts of second-degree assault with a deadly weapon and one count of falsely reporting a crime in connection with the Jan. 14 incident that occurred during Operation Metro Surge in the Twin Cities.

Following the incident, the Department of Homeland Security claimed an officer fired a “defensive shot” after being attacked by three men with a snow shovel and broom handle. One of those men was Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, who was hit in the thigh and taken to the hospital.

Authorities have alleged Castro lied about the circumstances of the shooting.

ICE has come under significant scrutiny after a string of shootings, several of which have been fatal.

Since President Trump took office, immigration officers have shot 23 people, killing six. Three of those deaths have been of U.S. citizens.

Federal authorities have also resisted cooperating with Minnesota officials following the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti.

Earlier this year, Minnesota state and county officials sued the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security to obtain records after the Trump administration said the FBI would buck precedent in not coordinating with local law enforcement.

articles.title: Miley Cyrus speaks after Dolly Parton’s death: ‘I will always love her and want to make her proud’
articles.summary: “I have an angel by my side. I always have.”
articles.body:
( KTLA ) — Miley Cyrus has broken her silence on the passing of her godmother , Dolly Parton, posting a heartfelt tribute on social media.

“The feeling of losing my Aunt Dolly is beyond what feels right to share. Our most sacred moments were private and they’ll stay there behind the stage, beneath the glamour & between our hearts,” the “Wrecking Ball” singer wrote on Instagram . “What I KNOW is Dolly would want me to feel it, write a song about it, and then continue on and be strong.”

“I have an angel by my side. I always have. One of our last conversations was about music and metamorphosis,” she added.

The two Tennessee natives have long had a strong bond, which developed before Cyrus was even born. Parton toured with the pop singer’s father, Billy Ray Cyrus, in 1992 as he promoted his hit single “Achy Breaky Heart.”

Miley Cyrus and Dolly Parton behind-the-scenes on the set of “Hannah Montana.” (Photo by Joel Warren/Disney Channel via Getty Images)

During the tour, rumors were swirling in the tabloids that the two were romantically linked. When Cyrus approached Parton about it, she quipped , “Honey, that’s what sells records.”

“From that moment we became friends,” he told journalist Dan Rather.

About 15 years later, Parton famously played Aunt Dolly in “Hannah Montana,” and both Miley and the country superstar hit it off. From then on, the actor and singer referred to Dolly as her godmother and fairy godmother.

Over the past 20 years, they collaborated several times. In 2017, Parton appeared on Miley’s song “Rainbowland.” The 11-time Grammy winner also performed a cover of Miley’s “Wrecking Ball.”

Just seven months ago, she re-recorded her hit “Light of a Clear Blue Morning” in collaboration with Cyrus, Queen Latifah, Reba McEntire and Lainey Wilson.

The “Flowers” singer ended her online tribute by saying, “I will always love her and want to make her proud. My heart breaks for the world, her family and friends who will miss her deeply. We’re in this loss together and we will see her in all of the most beautiful things.”

Parton passed away on Tuesday after a brief battle with cancer. Her death comes a little over a year after her husband of nearly 60 years, Carl Thomas Dean, passed away.

She is survived by her numerous nieces and nephews, and several siblings.

articles.title: Mamdani ignites online firestorm after mourning death of inmate charged in grisly murder: 'WTF are we doing?'
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's post mourning Clarence Woodward, a murder suspect who died on Rikers Island, sparked conservative outrage.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani drew ire from conservatives on Tuesday for mourning the death of a man who was awaiting trial on murder charges. "I am deeply saddened by the death of a New Yorker in City custody at a jail on Rikers Island early this morning," Mamdani posted on X. Clarence Woodward, the man Mamdani was referencing, was arrested in 2024 and charged with murder, manslaughter and assault in connection with an unprovoked meat cleaver attack at a Bronx laundromat. At the time, Woodward had 27 prior arrests and had received parole just a month prior to the alleged killing. Woodward had pleaded not guilty to the charges and had not been convicted. "My thoughts are with his family and loved ones as they grieve this loss. We do not yet know the cause of death, but we do know that too many New Yorkers have died on Rikers Island. The Department of Correction and its oversight partners will investigate the circumstances surrounding his death. Our administration is fully committed to the critical work of creating better conditions in our city’s jail system and closing Rikers Island as quickly as possible." WOKE LANGUAGE OVERHAUL WOULD STRIP THE WORD 'INMATE' FROM NEW YORK CITY'S ENTIRE JAIL RULEBOOK As of Thursday morning, Mamdani’s post has been viewed over 3.2 million times, with the majority of comments expressing outrage over Mamdani offering condolences to the inmate. "I wonder if he was ‘deeply saddened’ by the murder this guy committed," New York City Councilwoman Vicky Paladino wrote. "Can’t find a tweet about that one." "He’s sad that someone who murdered an innocent American with a meat cleaver is dead," conservative commentator Eyal Yakoby posted. "What are we even doing?" DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS SEIZE THE MOMENT WITH EXTREME, ANTI-AMERICAN VIEWS THAT BADLY TARNISH THE PARTY "Commie Mamdani is ‘deeply saddened’ that a guy who murdered a guy with a meat cleaver had a medical emergency in jail," failed Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt said in response to the post. "We cannot have leaders who weep for murderers. WTF are we doing?" "A father of two was hacked to death with a meat cleaver after his killer was repeatedly paroled," GOP strategist and attorney Mehek Cooke posted on X. "And you think the real villain is the jail?" The criticism comes weeks after Mamdani faced similar backlash for visiting Rikers Island, where he spoke with inmates during a World Cup semifinal watch party in July. While conservatives on social media were unhappy with Mamdani’s statement, officials and community activists have long raised concerns about the conditions on Rikers Island. Many, for instance, point out that many of the individuals being held there are awaiting trial and thus entitled to a presumption of innocence. "​​Our people are dying while under the custody of the Department of Corrections from medical neglect, physical abuse and unsafe conditions," one community activist said in June 2025 about Rikers Island. "People shouldn't keep dying in the same facility while awaiting a fair trial," the chief research editor of Rolling Stone magazine wrote on X. DEMOCRATIC SENATE CANDIDATE CALLED FOR MASS RELEASE OF CRIMINALS DURING PRISON ABOLITION WEBINAR New York City has been legally committed since 2019 to closing Rikers and replacing it with four smaller borough-based jails, a plan Mamdani has pledged to accelerate. Critics argue the move would leave the city with fewer jail cells and make it more difficult to tackle crime. "On the same day Mamdani was mourning a murderer who had a medical emergency in jail, another murderer was out taking more innocent lives after NYC leftists cut him loose early despite at least a dozen prior arrests and a history of violent crime," Heritage Foundation president Kevin Roberts posted, referencing a parolee police were seeking in connection with two deadly robberies in Brooklyn and the Bronx. articles.title: Rhode Island governor trails challenger in new Democratic primary poll
articles.summary: Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee (D) is trailing his challenger Helena Foulkes ahead of the upcoming Democratic gubernatorial primary, according to a new poll. The survey from Emerson College Polling and Nexstar affiliate WPRI-TV 12 shows Foulkes with a 15-point lead over the incumbent. The former CVS health official garnered 45 percent support to McKee’s…
articles.body:
Rhode Island Gov. Dan McKee (D) is trailing his challenger Helena Foulkes ahead of the upcoming Democratic gubernatorial primary, according to a new poll.

The survey from Emerson College Polling and Nexstar affiliate WPRI-TV 12 shows Foulkes with a 15-point lead over the incumbent. The former CVS health official garnered 45 percent support to McKee’s 30 percent. Another 25 percent of respondents were undecided.

“Governor McKee has a base among primary voters without a college degree (61 percent) and union members (40 percent), but not enough at this point to overtake Foulkes’ plurality support among voters over 50, at 48 percent,” said Spencer Kimball, executive director of Emerson College Polling.

McKee, who is 75 years old , recently endorsed a new policy called the “Rule of 90,” which would allow individuals older than 60 to receive full retirement benefits if they’ve completed 30 years of government service.

The governor says if he’s reelected, he will include the policy in his 2028 fiscal budget, according to the Rhode Island Current .

Meanwhile, Foulkes has embraced affordability messaging with a plan to pour $100 million into career and technical education facilities across the state if elected. The ex-health executive also plans to raise Medicaid reimbursement rates, ease COVID-19 restrictions for healthcare providers and expedite licenses for providers.

“In my 25-year career at CVS, I learned firsthand just how difficult it is for most Americans to navigate our broken healthcare system,” she said in a statement on her website . “But I also learned that by focusing on people’s needs, we can save money, improve health outcomes, and save lives.”

“For example, under my leadership we implemented a program to ensure that every CVS customer could access the lowest price for the prescriptions, even if it wasn’t through their insurance,” Foulkes continued. “The insurance companies didn’t like it one bit, but it was the right thing to do.”

While Foulkes is leading in the August poll, McKee has earned more support since the last survey in May. Support for the incumbent increased by 10 percentage points, compared with a 5 percent change for his challenger.

The Emerson College Polling/WPRI-TV 12 survey of likely Rhode Island voters was conducted from Aug. 21-22. It has a margin of error of 3 percentage points.
