articles.title: Can ethics issues tip party control of Congress?
articles.summary: While Democratic consultants urge candidates to focus on the economy, foreign policy, and government ethics ahead of the midterms, bipartisan leaders are working to streamline the House ethics process despite skepticism regarding potential partisan abuse.
articles.body:
A Democratic campaign consultant recently said he was urging his clients to emphasize three themes in their election fights against Republicans: first, the economy, including the affordability of such things as food, fuel, healthcare and housing; second, the war in Iran, including the lack of coherent objectives and goals, and its seeming interminability; and third, ethics in government — the sexual and financial scandals in Congress and the executive branch.

I have previously opined that the recent spike in congressional sexual misconduct cases, mostly involving members’ office staff, may affect the outcomes in those specific districts and races, but will not have a disproportionate impact on one party or the other nationally. Sexual misconduct is an equal-opportunity destroyer.

In looking over ethics cases in this Congress, there are slightly more Republicans than Democrats who have been tainted by ethics scandals. The unethical conduct charges being hurled at the administration, on the other hand, involving conflicts of interest, financial self-dealing, and use of law enforcement against political enemies, are legion. These do not seem to bother the public as much as sex scandals, but they can become a factor when the public perceives their cumulative effects on good governance.

Still, the odoriferous vapors rising inside the beltway cannot be ruled out as irrelevant to the upcoming midterm elections. It’s not just the smell of blooming algae and peeling blue paint fumes from the reflecting pool (though those do have a whiff of a no-bid contract vandal scandal ). The economics-ethics link could put Republicans at a serious electoral disadvantage this November.

How does the party that effectively controls all three branches fight back against these perceived ethical lapses? We have been through this before, every two decades or so, and the natural responses by those in power is: reform. I am reminded of one old congressional codger who had been up and down this hill so many times that he cried in exasperation, “Reform, reform, reform; that’s all we hear. As if things weren’t bad enough already.”

The motivation to reform under current circumstances is a natural response, though it is no guarantee of changing the image and behavior of Congress. One cannot hope to rejuvenate or eradicate all the bad apples in the barrel, let alone be cheered on from skeptical citizens on the sidelines.

But there are some signs of hope. A bipartisan effort is being made by Reps. Kat Cammack (R-Fla.) and Teresa Leger Fernandez (D-N.M.), chairs of their respective parties’ women’s caucuses, to present recommendations when the House reconvenes next month for streamlining the ethics process and making it more accessible for staff to report violations. The two lawmakers have the full support of Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) to pursue their reform efforts — offering them considerable legitimacy. Nevertheless, there are skeptics in the House who fear any reforms may open the door to frivolous or false complaints for partisan advantage.

The so-called ethics wars are not a recent development, and separating the wheat from the chaff has always been a major challenge for the Ethics Committee. Previous attempts to ensure full and thorough investigations while protecting accused members’ rights to due process have created so many built-in safeguards that timely action by the committee has often been stymied, especially with a backlog of complaints pending.

As a rule, an Ethics Committee report cannot be issued after a member has resigned since the House no longer has jurisdiction over that member and any findings or recommended punishment. The one exception made to that rule was in 2024 when Rep. Matt Gaetz (R-Fla.) resigned from the House in November when nominated by President Trump for attorney general. Even though Gaetz withdrew his nomination a week later, the House Ethics committee still issued its adverse report on his conduct in December .

In late July 2026, just before the summer recess, House Republicans tried to inoculate themselves on a legitimate ethics conundrum by passing a bill that purported to bar members and their families from insider stock trading. But the bill had more holes in it than a bag of donuts. It was reported from the House Administration Committee on a straight party-line vote, and then passed the House, 232 to 198 , with only 13 Democrats voting in favor. It’s reportedly dead-on-arrival in the Senate.

Ethics games are less vicious than ethics wars, but they still send mixed signals to voters about how serious members are about policing themselves.

Don Wolfensberger is a 28-year congressional staff veteran, culminating as chief of staff of the House Rules Committee. He is author of, “Congress and the People: Deliberative Democracy on Trial” (2000), and, “Changing Cultures in Congress: From Fair Play to Power Plays” (2018).

Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick D-Fla., is seen at the House Ethics Committee during a hearing originally scheduled to consider sanctions against former Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick D-Fla., on Capitol Hill in Washington, Tuesday, April 21, 2026. Cherfilus-McCormick resigned from Congress shortly before the hearing was set to begin. (AP Photo/Jose Luis Magana)

articles.title: Democratic strategist: ‘Something’s going on’ when Trump ‘can only deliver 52 percent’ in South Carolina
articles.summary: Democratic strategist Chuck Rocha said Wednesday he expected President Trump’s endorsement of Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) to lead to a wider margin of victory for her in Tuesday’s GOP Senate runoff. Rocha explained in an appearance on NewsNation’s “Cuomo” that he thought Graham would win but “didn’t think it would be this close” given Trump…
articles.body:
Democratic strategist Chuck Rocha said Wednesday he expected President Trump’s endorsement of Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) to lead to a wider margin of victory for her in Tuesday’s GOP Senate runoff.

Rocha explained in an appearance on NewsNation’s “Cuomo” that he thought Graham would win but “didn’t think it would be this close” given Trump backed the senator.

She defeated Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) by just less than 5 points in the state’s runoff, securing a spot on the general election ballot in place of her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

The GOP nominee will now face Democrat Annie Andrews in the general election , with Decision Desk HQ giving the Republican an 81 percent chance to win as of Tuesday.

Rocha, who advised Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) during his two unsuccessful presidential campaigns, noted that Darline Graham’s narrow runoff victory does not lead him to believe Andrews will win.

“But I am going to say something’s going on when Donald Trump can only deliver 52 percent,” he told host Chris Cuomo, while qualifying, “I get it was a special election. She’s only been running a little bit.”

The strategist also noted more than 40 percent of voters in June’s GOP primary voted for a candidate other than Lindsey Graham, an election held just more than a month before the four-term senator died of an aortic dissection .

“But Donald Trump should be getting 70, 80, 90 percent in a Republican primary,” Rocha argued.

The president hit the trail last week to stump for Darline Graham, venturing to the coastal town of Myrtle Beach, S.C. During a rally alongside the newest senator, he urged Republicans to turn out in the midterms.

“What I want you to do is pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” Trump said at the time.

Graham won Horry County , where Myrtle Beach is located, by more than 46 points over Norman. The senator was also victorious in 34 of 46 counties in the Palmetto State, according to data from the South Carolina Election Commission.

The victory was seen as a significant flex by Trump after Graham made a major gaffe a week earlier on the debate state while dodging a question about Taiwan and the South China Sea.

More than 369,000 Republicans in the state cast a ballot in the runoff, accounting for roughly 12 percent of the more than 3 million total registered voters in the state, per the state election commission .

Democrats have suggested Graham’s win could give their party a chance at taking the seat, though that appears unlikely.

Conservative talk show host Mark Davis, who also appeared as a guest on Cuomo’s show, defended the GOP hopeful as being the “deep underdog” in the race “because nobody knew who she was on July 10, the day before Lindsey died.”

“For Trump to endorse her and bring her across the finish line is a major, major bit of evidence to the strength of his endorsement,” he added.

articles.title: Michigan Dem AG turns on El-Sayed over terror attack response, warns of mentality that 'bothers me a lot'
articles.summary: Dana Nessel says Abdul El-Sayed's response to the Temple Israel attack appeared to make excuses for domestic terrorism targeting Jewish worshippers.
articles.body: Michigan's Democratic Attorney General Dana Nessel is voicing concerns about her party’s Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, saying his response to the attempted terrorist attack on a Michigan synagogue appeared to make excuses for "domestic terrorism" as she warns about increasing anti-Israel sentiments in her party. Nessel, Michigan’s attorney general since 2019, spoke at length in an interview with The Atlantic’s David Frum about her position that she doesn’t feel safe as a Jewish person attending her own state party’s convention due in part to "an enormous amount of anti-Semitism within the Democratic Party." Nessel specifically took issue with El-Sayed’s response to the synagogue attack in Michigan earlier this year when federal investigators say a gunman inspired and radicalized by Hezbollah crashed into the place of worship seeking to kill as many Jewish people as he could. "But, you know, the reaction to it, obviously there’s a lot of people who were quick to call this out. But, you know, I think most concerning, of course, was the statement that our nominee for U.S. Senate made, which was that ‘hurt people hurt people,’" Nessel explained. "And a lot of us perceived that as sort of making excuses for somebody who sought to murder over 100 pre-K schoolchildren. And that’s the kind of mentality that bothers me a lot." MICHIGAN'S DEMOCRATIC AG REFUSES TO ATTEND UPCOMING CONVENTION OVER HARASSMENT CONCERNS Nessel went on to reflect on how she responded to the 2019 Christchurch mosque massacre by visiting a Dearborn mosque, wearing a hijab out of respect and unequivocally condemning Islamophobia. She contrasted that response with El-Sayed’s reaction to the Temple Israel attack. "I didn’t try to get into, like, what were the motivations of the person who killed these people, and did he have mental-health issues?" Nessel said. "Did he have bad experiences with Muslims? I just condemned it unequivocally, and I think that’s what people should have done with Temple Israel. You can’t make excuses for that kind of domestic terrorism." Nessel credited El-Sayed for his outreach to Jewish leaders in recent months but expressed the belief that he should publicly retract his comments in the aftermath of the attack. ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE REACHES DEADLIEST LEVEL SINCE 1994, NEW GLOBAL REPORT FINDS "I think privately, he will say that he regrets having made those remarks," Nessel said. "But here we are, it’s almost the end of August, and he still has not withdrawn those statements and said, I misspoke, or, I now recognize the harm that I caused by making those statements. And it has me concerned that he really stands by them." Nessel urged El-Sayed to acknowledge he was wrong, listen to Jewish stakeholders and publicly change course, as she said she has done when confronted with her own past ignorance. She said she has also urged him to better understand Jewish religious beliefs, pointing to his post-primary reference to "breaking bread with Jews at Passover," when bread is intentionally not eaten during the holiday. "But I asked, could you learn a little bit more about our religion so that you understand it?" Nessel said. "Could you learn a little bit more than maybe what your bubble is telling you about the history of Israel and its relationship to the Jewish people?" And again, I leave room for the fact that all of us have the opportunity to learn more." Nessel made it clear that she is not planning to support the state's Republican Senate candidate, Mike Rogers, and that she would "amputate [her] right arm" before voting for him because "keeping a Republican majority in the Senate is incredibly dangerous." "With Abdul, I will say this: We have a lot in common in terms of our general beliefs and principles and policies," Nessel said. Trust me; I have much more in common with Abdul El-Sayed than I do with Mike Rogers in terms of my personal beliefs, my political beliefs, my philosophical beliefs about what should happen in the United States, and in the United States Senate." "To my Jewish sisters and brothers, you have a right to worship in peace," El-Sayed said. "You have a right to send your kids to the synagogue in the morning and know they’ll come home safely at night. And you have a right to know that your religious identity and faith practice are respected. There is no room for antisemitism in America. So today and everyday, I am standing in solidarity with all of us who value our right to pray how we choose to pray against antisemitism and hate in all its forms." articles.title: Amid a physician shortage, we’re making medical school harder to afford
articles.summary: At the very moment our nation needs more doctors, federal policy may be making it more difficult for talented young people to become one.
articles.body:
Americans already wait weeks — and in some communities, months — to see a physician. At the very moment our nation needs more doctors, federal policy may be making it more difficult for talented young people to become one.

New federal limits on student borrowing are taking effect, creating unintended consequences that extend far beyond medical schools. Unless Congress and the administration revisit these restrictions, we risk worsening an already critical physician shortage, reducing access to care and narrowing the pipeline of future physicians.

Supporters of these borrowing limits make legitimate points. They argue that unlimited federal lending has contributed to tuition inflation, encouraged excessive borrowing and shifted too much financial risk to taxpayers. They also believe colleges should have stronger incentives to control costs. Those are reasonable policy objectives.

Medical education, however, is fundamentally different from nearly every other graduate program.

Under the 2025 federal budget reconciliation law , medical students are generally limited to borrowing $50,000 annually and $200,000 over the course of their professional education, subject to a $257,500 aggregate federal borrowing limit. While many currently enrolled students are protected, these limits will increasingly affect future applicants deciding whether medicine remains financially attainable.

Unlike most graduate students, physicians enter one of the nation’s most workforce-constrained professions, complete years of supervised residency training and have historically demonstrated exceptionally low student loan default rates. Applying the same financing model to medical education risks solving one problem while creating another: producing fewer physicians precisely when America needs more.

The timing could not be worse. The Health Resources and Services Administration projects a shortage of more than 141,000 physicians by 2038. Americans already struggle to access primary care, behavioral health services and many specialties, particularly in rural and underserved communities.

Every physician who enters practice represents an investment that pays dividends for decades through improved health, stronger communities and greater economic productivity. Yet the financial realities of becoming a physician have changed dramatically.

A recent Journal of the American Medical Association study found that the percentage of medical students requiring federal loans above these new limits has risen substantially over the past decade. The financing model established by Congress simply no longer reflects today’s cost of medical education.

The solution is not as simple as telling medical schools to reduce tuition.

Medical schools have a responsibility to control costs, and many are doing exactly that. Many institutions, including my own, have kept tuition increases below inflation while continuing to invest in simulation technology, cybersecurity, student support and the regulatory requirements necessary to educate highly competent physicians.

But tuition is only part of the equation. Housing, food, transportation, health insurance and childcare have risen sharply. Medical school is a full-time commitment that leaves little opportunity for outside employment. For many students, living expenses equal — or exceed — the cost of tuition.

Students with family wealth or parents able to co-sign loans will likely find financing. Others will not.

Those most likely to be affected are often those our healthcare system needs most: students from rural communities, first-generation college families, military veterans and individuals from historically underrepresented backgrounds. These physicians are more likely to practice in underserved communities. When financial barriers discourage them, patients ultimately pay the price.

Private lenders are beginning to fill part of the financing gap, but access increasingly depends on creditworthiness rather than academic merit or a student’s commitment to serve. Opportunity should be determined by ability, character and commitment — not by family wealth or access to credit.

Medical students represent one of the strongest lending investments in higher education. Medical school graduates have among the lowest student loan default rates of any professional group, reflecting stable employment and a long history of repayment. The Association of American Medical Colleges reports that medical school borrowers have near-zero default rates , while federal data place default rates for the broader category of professional degree borrowers at approximately 1.5 percent .

Communities, philanthropists, health systems and universities are expanding scholarships and developing innovative financing programs. These efforts are commendable, but they cannot replace a predictable and sustainable federal financing system.

For decades, our nation has viewed medical education as an investment in the public good. That principle should not change because the economics of higher education have changed.

If we are serious about strengthening our physician workforce and improving access to care, we should not erect new financial barriers for qualified students willing to dedicate their lives to caring for others.

Congress and the administration should revisit these borrowing limits before they become a long-term obstacle to developing the physicians our nation urgently needs.

The U.S. has never solved a workforce shortage by making entry into that profession more difficult. Medicine should be no exception.

America cannot solve its physician shortage by making it harder to become a physician.

Marc B. Hahn is president and chief executive officer of Kansas City University. A board-certified anesthesiologist, he has spent more than four decades in medical education preparing the nation’s future physicians, including service as a U.S. Army physician.

articles.title: Blood moon lunar eclipse: This is the best time to watch in every state
articles.summary: At maximum, the full moon will be 96% covered by Earth’s shadow, turning it a spooky shade of red.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – You’ll want to look up Thursday night to catch a glimpse of the blood moon lunar eclipse , which will be visible (at least in part) across all of North America.

At maximum, the full moon will be 96% covered by Earth’s shadow, turning it a spooky shade of red. While it’s just a few percentage points behind a total lunar eclipse, the view will still be pretty impressive. The best time to see it depends on where you live.

The most dramatic time to see the lunar eclipse is when it’s at maximum Thursday night or early Friday morning. That happens at a different time in every time zone:

There’s another phase of the eclipse not listed on the chart above called the penumbral eclipse, which starts about an hour before the partial eclipse begins and ends an hour after the partial eclipse concludes. This phase of the eclipse is more subtle. It happens when the moon moves through the outer part of Earth’s shadow, or its penumbra.

The view gets better as the moon moves into the umbra, or the main part of the Earth’s shadow. That will start at around 10:30 p.m. Eastern Time during the partial eclipse phase.

Finally, when the eclipse is at maximum, nearly all of the moon will be covered by Earth’s shadow, scattering blue light waves and turning the moon red.

Not everyone will get the same view of the eclipse. Those in time zones further east will likely have a better view as the moon will be higher up in the sky.

The sun sets too late in Hawaii and Alaska to really get the best view of the eclipse maximum, but people in both states may be able to catch the tail end of the eclipse if they look to the moon shortly after sunset.

Rep. Jimmy Patronis (R-Fla.) ripped country star Jason DeFord, whose stage name is Jelly Roll, after the singer’s late-night monologue made fun of President Trump’s weight, with Patronis saying the singer is no longer welcome in his Florida Panhandle district.

Jelly Roll returned as a guest host on ABC’s “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” Monday night, where he poked fun at Trump’s weight. The rapper-turned-country singer said he had shed 300 pounds, comparing that weight loss to “an entire Donald Trump.”

“And let’s be honest, based on his approval ratings , it seems like most of the country wants to do the same thing,” he said.

He continued, “From one fat pig to another, take it from me that physical fitness is very important. Trust me, you’ll be happy to see your penis again.”

Several of Trump’s allies, including Patronis, were outraged on social media about Jelly Roll’s monologue.

Jelly Roll “is 100% not welcomed to Florida’s panhandle,” Patronis wrote on the social platform X . “I don’t even want to see his bus on I-10. He’s always been the token ‘country’ star the libs in California are allowed to enjoy. (He ain’t country, never was.).”

“Take the TDS elsewhere, loser,” he added, referring to “Trump Derangement Syndrome.”

Jelly Roll responded to the backlash from his monologue on Tuesday’s episode , joking that he never thought he would get in more trouble with the president than actress Rosie O’Donnell, who has famously feuded with Trump for years.

“Any U.S. president should be able to handle a few jokes, right?” Jelly Roll said.

The singer has been quiet about his political affiliation in the past, but he hyped up the president’s move to host a UFC event on the White House South Lawn to commemorate the country’s 250th birthday.

Last year, Jelly Roll stirred headlines after testifying on Capitol Hill about the fentanyl crisis.

“At every concert I perform, I witness the heartbreaking impact of fentanyl,” he told lawmakers. “I see fans grappling with this tragedy in the form of music, that they seek solace in music and hope that their experiences won’t befall others.”

Jelly Roll was pardoned in December by Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee (R) after he was convicted of robbery in 2005 as a juvenile and broke parole. He was found with cocaine in his possession, and he was charged with intent to sell.

After being released from prison in 2016, the Tennessee Board of Parole unanimously recommended his pardon in early 2025.

articles.title: A Trump North Korea deal
articles.summary: President Donald Trump aims to restart direct negotiations with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un to secure verifiable limits on nuclear programs and end North Korea’s support for Russia’s war in Ukraine.
articles.body:
President Trump ordered the reduction of ongoing U.S.-South Korea military exercises last week. He also wants to meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un . These are the least surprising developments of Trump’s second term; the only real surprise is that it took this long.

In his first term, Trump used his unconventional approach to foreign policy to break the stalemate of more than 20 years of failed diplomacy with North Korea. His three predecessors (two Democrats and a Republican) basically pursued the same policy: sanctions, sanctions relief and incentives provided to the Kim family to forgo its nuclear weapons aspirations.

Former Presidents Bill Clinton and George W. Bush negotiated different versions of the same deal with Kim Il Sung and Kim Jong Il, the grandfather and father of the current North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Those deals allowed Pyongyang to easily reverse constraints on its nuclear program if Kim wanted to pressure Washington or after a change in administrations.

Trump turned this approach on its head by executing a maximum pressure policy that strangled Kim’s economy and even forced China to close North Korea’s bank accounts , an unprecedented move. Trump also met directly with Kim Jong Un which rejected the Clinton, Bush and Obama approach of using China as a mediator and negotiating with lower-level North Korean officials. North Korea decision making is centralized in its leader, Trump cut out the middlemen to embrace that reality.

Unfortunately, Trump enters potential negotiations with Kim in a weaker position than in his first term. Former President Biden publicly condemned Pyongyang’s assistance to Russia for its war in Ukraine but did little to stop it or force Kim to choose between helping Russian President Vladimir Putin and his own strategic programs.

Trump could restore leverage against Kim by sanctioning North Koreans operating in China and Chinese companies and individuals who are aiding Pyongyang’s sanctions evasion. These actions would not disrupt Trump’s approach with Chinese leader Xi Jinping because they are similar to U.S. efforts targeting Chinese teapot refineries processing Iranian oil.

The president’s bold action to strike Iran’s threshold nuclear weapons program last year in the Midnight Hammer strikes and subsequent military strikes this year provides him additional flexibility. Negotiations with Kim will likely include at least a tacit acknowledgement of North Korea’s nuclear weapons program. Tehran would have seen that as a green light to pursue its own nuclear weapons. But the Islamic Republic is in dire financial danger and there are questions on whether it can survive in the long term.

America’s allies and partners could see acceptance of North Korea’s nuclear weapons as a signal that a future administration would accept development of their own nuclear arsenals. But Washington retains incentives and disincentives to prevent those programs.

Negotiating a deal with North Korea will not be easy. While many see Pyongyang as a backwards Hermit Kingdom, they have over three decades of experience negotiating with the United States and have largely won those encounters.

In addition to Washington’s acceptance of North Korea’s nuclear program, Trump could offer a peace treaty formally ending the Korean War, a better political and economic relationship, and a permanent end to military exercises with South Korea. He could also facilitate future North Korea-South Korea negotiations.

Trump should insist on verifiable limits on Pyongyang’s long-range ballistic missile and nuclear weapons programs. And any deal would need to include North Korea withdrawing all troops and military assistance for Russia’s war in Ukraine.

He would be able to add to his growing list of diplomatic achievements ending conflicts in his second term and weaken Putin in the process potentially leading to a negotiated settlement between Moscow and Kyiv. Trump could also eventually travel to North Korea or a neutral site to sign a deal with Kim which would be another made-for-TV moment in his presidency.

Trump will be criticized for this approach, but he should be commended for pursuing an achievable goal rather than pursuing the same negotiations strategy and expecting a different result.

Anthony Ruggiero is a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council. He was National Security Council director for North Korea and deputy assistant to President Trump and senior director for counterproliferation and biodefense.

Since assuming power 10 years ago, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has ruled the isolated country with absolute power, significantly expanded its nuclear arsenal and become the North’s first ruler to hold a summit with a sitting U.S. president. But now, he’s hunkering down and struggling to revive a dilapidated economy battered hard by pandemic-related border shutdowns, toughened U.N. sanctions and mismanagement. articles.body:
President Trump on Wednesday named Mark Paoletta the chair of the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC), a panel overseeing his White House ballroom and Washington arch projects.

Paoletta, the general counsel of the White House Office of Management and Budget, will succeed Will Scharf as chair of the NCPC. Scharf is set to take over for David Warrington as White House counsel Monday.

The 12-member NCPC acts as the federal government’s planning agency for projects in the D.C. region. The commission is involved in the “planning, policymaking and project review” processes, specifically reviewing the design of federal and “certain” local projects, according to its website .

Panelists on the NCPC in April approved Trump’s plan to build a ballroom where the demolished East Wing once stood. Construction crews first tore down the East Wing in October, with the White House saying the ballroom will be done before the end of the president’s term.

Chief Justice John Roberts last week temporarily blocked a lower court ruling halting the project, in a case brought by the National Trust for Historic Preservation nonprofit.

The order from Roberts gave the Supreme Court additional time to consider the Trump administration’s emergency appeal of the lower-court ruling.

In July, the NCPC also approved a preliminary site and building plans for a 250-foot triumphal arch Trump has proposed. The arch would be constructed near Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia, just across the Potomac River from the nation’s capital.

Scharf, the then-chair of the planning commission, said at the time a final vote will take place in September on whether the arch could bypass a federal law limiting building heights in D.C. to 130 feet.

In a statement, Paoletta said the president “has transformed D.C. into a capital worthy of the greatest nation in history,” according to The New York Times .

“I look forward to working with my new colleagues to further the president’s historic restoration and beautification of the National Capital Region, especially in the 250th year of our country’s independence,” he added.

In addition to his role at the Office of Management and Budget, Paoletta has been the acting director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau since the start of this month. Trump has nominated Brian Johnson to serve as the full-time head of the consumer protection agency, which the administration has sought to dismantle .

A close associate of Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas, Paoletta represented his wife, Ginni Thomas, while the House Select Committee on the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol probed her.

articles.title: What is up with the controversial ‘mega’ immigration court hearings?
articles.summary: Mega master calendar hearings will only reduce the backlog if they produce legally sustainable orders.
articles.body:
The current administration is the only one in more than a decade that has succeeded in reducing the country’s immigration court backlog. A Justice Department official recently told KPBS public broadcasting of San Diego that , “Reducing the immigration court backlog remains one of the highest priorities for this administration.”

The backlog rose every year from fiscal 2013 through fiscal 2024, when it reached a record high of 3,716,106 cases. The Trump administration reversed this uninterrupted increase in in fiscal 2025, when it reduced the backlog to 3,416, 921 cases. As of today, it has reduced the number of cases to 3,195,137.

The immigration court is still overwhelmed , of course, but the administration is finding additional ways to reduce the backlog. In May 2026 , it increased the number of aliens at master calendar hearings from 20 to 30 aliens to up to 150. These hearings, referred to as “mega master calendar hearings,” have made it possible to issue a record number of in absentia removal orders — that is, in the alien’s absence — from 35,000 in May to 54,000 in June.

Master calendar hearings are not trials to determine deportability, asylum eligibility or eligibility for other forms of relief that require trials. Master calendar hearings are held for pleadings, scheduling merits hearings, advising aliens of their rights, explaining the charges in their Notice to Appear and other similar matters.

Notice of a master calendar hearing is sent to the address that the alien provided. Aliens in removal proceedings are required to provide the immigration court with their address and telephone number and to report any changes. The hearing date in the notice must be at least 10 days after service of the notice to give the alien time to retain counsel.

If an alien fails to appear at a hearing in removal proceedings, he or she “shall be ordered removed in absentia if [ICE] establishes by clear, unequivocal, and convincing evidence that the written notice was so provided and that the alien is removable.”

Immigration advocates claim that mega master calendar hearings are being used to rush aliens through removal proceedings instead of letting them have a merits hearing at which they could apply for relief from deportation. Maybe, but if an alien in removal proceedings has not kept the immigration court informed of their address, the court will not be able to contact them when a merits hearing becomes available. So aliens who don’t provide their address will be subject to absentia proceedings either way.

Aliens cannot appeal an absentia removal order, but they can file a motion asking the immigration judge to reopen the proceedings to rescind the order. A motion to rescind an absentia removal order must be filed within 180 days of when the removal order was served. If it is based on allegations of not receiving notice of the hearing or on being in federal or state custody, it may be filed at any time.

The alien can appeal a denial of his motion to the Board of Immigration Appeals . And board decisions can be challenged in federal court.

Issues most likely to be litigated include the following:

Hearing notice: Sending a hearing notice to the last address provided by the alien raises a presumption that it was delivered, but the alien can overcome the presumption with evidence that it was not delivered. The alien also can claim that the failure to appear was due to exceptional circumstances, to not receiving proper notice, or to being held in federal or state custody, and that the failure to appear was not his fault.

Right to counsel: The Board of Immigration Appeals recently held that the prohibition on scheduling a master calendar earlier than 10 days after service of the hearing notice is the only fixed statutory or regulatory timing requirement for protecting the alien’s right to counsel at no expense to the government. However, the immigration judge can grant a continuance to give the alien more time for good cause. If a continuance is denied and the outcome of the proceeding is a removal order, the alien can challenge the denial with a motion to reopen proceedings to rescind the order.

The absentia removal order. A removal order cannot be based solely on an alien’s failure to appear at the hearing. The Department of Homeland Security has to establish that proper hearing notice was given and that removability was based on clear, unequivocal and convincing evidence. These findings can be challenged in a motion to reopen, an appeal to the board, or an appeal of the board’s decision to a federal court.

Litigation can be reduced by ensuring that immigration judges have the training needed to conduct in absentia proceedings properly and that the hearings are fair and conducted without due process violations. Mega master calendar hearings will only reduce the backlog if they produce legally sustainable orders.

Nolan Rappaport was detailed to the House Judiciary Committee as an executive branch immigration law expert for three years. He subsequently served as an immigration counsel for the Subcommittee on Immigration, Border Security and Claims for four years. Prior to working on the Judiciary Committee, he wrote decisions for the Board of Immigration Appeals for 20 years. Follow his blog at .

articles.title: Hannity: Trump ‘is on the ballot’ in midterms

Hannity told viewers, “Let me explain this: He is on the ballot because if we don’t get Republicans in the House and Senate,…
articles.body:
Fox News host Sean Hannity on Wednesday said President Trump is on the ballot for the midterms, a talking point that’s been hammered by strategists, lawmakers and voters alike throughout campaign season.

Hannity told viewers, “Let me explain this: He is on the ballot because if we don’t get Republicans in the House and Senate, all progress in this country will come to a screeching halt.”

The host warned that Trump and Republican officials could face impeachment trials under a Democratic majority in either the House or the Senate.

“Now, of course, if Democrats take back majorities in the House and Senate in the fall, impeaching Donald Trump, that will be our future again and again and again. That will be their top agenda item,” Hannity said.

“Then, implementing their radical agenda, as laid out on the DSA [Democratic Socialists of America] website. That’s why, in an exclusive interview with our friend Trey Gowdy, the president urged Americans to vote like he is on the ballot,” he added.

The GOP has majorities in both chambers, but it has faced some legislative pushback from among its ranks over the past year.

Trump has made an intentional effort to oust incumbents who have bucked his agenda, successfully unseating Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) and Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.).

He’s also aided Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) in gaining the party nomination to permanently retain the seat vacated by her late brother, telling voters to “pretend” he was on the ballot.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) says the president will do the same thing next month at the midterm convention.

“We’re going to talk about what we’ve done for the people. And then the president’s going to look right into the camera and say, I am on the ballot. OK,” Johnson emphasized during remarks at a campaign event for Rep. Monica De La Cruz (R-Texas).

“Because even though his name isn’t, right, his administration, his legacy, the ‘America First’ agenda is. We’ve got to get people to turn out,” he continued.

Trump has a 100 percent success rate for Senate campaign endorsements, according to Decision Desk HQ.

He has a 95 percent success rate for House races and a 69 percent success rate for gubernatorial races.

Hannity said under Trump’s leadership and a Republican majority, “We will get the government we deserve.”

“Sixty-nine days matter. I hope you will commit in your heart, mind, and soul that this is important, and we need to stop this right dead in its tracks,” Hannity added.

articles.title: Meta settles lawsuit, pays $17.1 billion over absurd claims
articles.summary: Busybodies in both parties long ago decided that Zuck was Public Enemy Number 1. And they are perfectly willing to erect a regime of mass censorship in order to get their man.
articles.body:
Zuck is cooked: his company has agreed to pay $17.1 billion to various states that sued Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, over allegations of harms to children.

Mark Zuckerberg evidently thought he was likely to lose, as the public sentiment has shifted so wildly against his company — it’s common to hear people assert as fact that it’s obvious Meta is harming children. That it’s some fact we all know, even though it’s highly disputed — and even dubious — what these so called harms are.

Make no mistake what’s happening here: The government is trying to decide for you, the parents, what level of access your children, your teenagers, are allowed to have to social media and tech, based on alleged harms that happened to someone else. I state again that the mass harms to children are entirely theoretical.

The states have taken the position that Meta’s products are designed to be addictive, so that kids will keep using them: They will keep scrolling on social media, and stay there.

But of course, the content on social media is just speech and expression, which is protected by the First Amendment. And young people have First Amendment rights too: They government can’t say, we don’t want you, a 16 year old, to read that book, because we think it’s bad for you. This has been litigated over and over again, and it’s the case that yes, young people enjoy this right too.

In order to get around this, the states argued that it’s not the content on Facebook that’s the problem, it’s the features: the recommendation algorithm, liking and sharing, photo manipulation, etc. So the states assert that those features are not protected speech, which is false, and also that they are definitely harmful, which is also false. Consider one such completely ridiculous argument, that Instagram’s filter feature, which allows you to touch up your pictures, is harming teenage girls because it makes other girls look too attractive and harms their self esteem.

What are we even doing here? Why on earth is this an issue for the state to decide?

Consider next the state’s claim that Meta knew about these harms and did nothing to warn people about them. This is patently ridiculous, as my Reason colleague Elizabeth Nolan Brown notes , because there is no persuasive evidence of harm.

She writes: “The states here argue that Meta was ‘deceptive’ by not telling people that social media would harm them. But given what we actually know, it would be deceptive for Meta to say that it would.”

That’s what this case is really about: The government wants to compel Zuckerberg to admit that his product is killing kids, when the evidence of pervasive harm is at best mixed. There’s tons of evidence, of course, that social media makes a positive difference in young people’s lives, by connecting them to their friends and to news and information — that occasional negative experiences are outweighed by positive ones.

But the government wants us to ignore all that, because busybodies in both parties long ago decided that Zuck was Public Enemy Number 1. And they are perfectly willing to erect a regime of mass censorship, based on misleading or cherry-picked statistics and nebulous applications of the word “harm,” in order to get their man .

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.body:
Former officials with the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) are urging a federal appeals court to reject the Trump administration’s attempts to ignore a long-standing presidential records retention requirement.

In an amicus brief filed Wednesday in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, six former archivists who worked under Republican and Democratic presidents pushed back on the Trump administration’s argument that the Presidential Records Act (PRA) of 1978 unconstitutionally infringes on the executive branch’s independence.

The NARA officials who signed on to the brief are former archivists Trudy Huskamp Peterson, John W. Carlin, David Ferriero, Debra Steidel Wall, Colleen Shogan and William Bosanko and former general counsel Gary M. Stern.

The filing supports an earlier lawsuit from historians and public transparency groups after the Department of Justice (DOJ) concluded in an April memo that the act “unconstitutionally intrudes on the independence and autonomy” of the executive branch and exceeds congressional authority.

U.S. District Judge John Bates ruled in May that White House staff must preserve official records amid ongoing litigation and determined the PRA was likely constitutional. The DOJ then appealed the ruling to the D.C. federal appeals court. Oral arguments are scheduled for Oct. 16.

The Hill has reached out to the White House and the DOJ for comment regarding the NARA officials’ filing.

Congress passed the law in 1978 following the Watergate scandal. It requires presidents and their staff to preserve White House records and turn them over to the National Archives when a head of state leaves office. The law applies to nonpersonal records created by the president, vice president and entities that “solely advise and assist” the executive.

The PRA played a central role in the 2023 case in which President Trump was accused of unlawfully keeping classified documents from his first term at his Florida Mar-a-Lago residence. He was indicted on 40 felony counts for alleged mishandling of these records, but the case was ultimately dropped following his reelection in 2024.

articles.title: Woefully underqualified: Darline Graham gives confusing victory speech
articles.summary: But if your own childhood demonstrates what happens when working families cannot afford to stop working when they’re sick, shouldn’t that make us want to fix the system?
articles.body:
President Trump helped propel Darline Graham from relative political obscurity into one of the most consequential Senate races in the country after the death of her brother, former Sen. Lindsey Graham.

After winning the Republican primary on Tuesday, Graham is asking South Carolina voters to give her a full six-year term in the U.S. Senate — but she seems completely unprepared for the job.

Take the subject of health care, for example.

During her victory speech, folks were confused when Graham attacked her Democratic opponent, pediatrician Dr. Annie Andrews, over her support for expanding access to affordable, high-quality health care. Graham shared a personal story in an attempt to prove that universal health care is a bad thing.

“My parents worked long hard hours to make ends meet,” she said. “We didn’t take vacations. If they were sick, they had to go to work because if the doors weren’t open, we weren’t making money. My mother passed away when I was 11 and my father just over a year later.”

Her story is heartbreaking. Her mother died of Hodgkin’s lymphoma at 51, and her father died roughly 15 months later after suffering a heart attack in his sleep. But if your own childhood demonstrates what happens when working families cannot afford to stop working when they’re sick, shouldn’t that make us want to fix the system?

Parents should have access to health care they can afford. People should be able to take time off when they’re sick without worrying that missing work means they can’t pay their bills. Graham’s anecdote was not a good argument against expanding health care access. It’s an argument for it.

In the richest country in the world, we can do much better than this. We should be working to build a health care system that gives families more options, more access and more security, not romanticizing the hardships that previous generations were forced to endure.

Because Darline Graham is the official Republican candidate, this race could be more competitive than people might assume.

Yes, South Carolina is a deeply Republican state. Trump carried it by more than 18 points in 2024. But Democrats see an opening with Graham as their opponent, particularly as Trump’s approval numbers have declined and voters continue to express frustration over the cost of living and the economy.

Andrews, who easily won the Democratic primary, has been raising significant money. Her most recent filing showed nearly $11 million raised and about $4 million cash on hand.

Graham has never been elected to public office. She was appointed to the Senate after her brother passed, and during the only debate of the Republican primary, she was asked about national security. You’ll remember her answer was remarkably bad . Ultimately, South Carolina voters are going to consider whether a famous last name, a presidential endorsement, and this response — “I’m just going to be honest here. I’m not on national security that I’m not that informed on national security” — is what they’re looking for in an elected official.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: Tariffs, the price of ground beef, and Donald Trump
articles.summary: Former President Trump’s proposal to temporarily pause tariffs on imported ground beef aims to lower prices before the midterm elections, despite economic analysis suggesting the 25 percent price reduction claim is unrealistic and potentially harmful to domestic producers.
articles.body:
President Trump is no economic Reaganite , the latest manifestation of which is his gambit to reduce the price of ground beef by pausing higher tariffs on 300,000 tons of imported ground beef for 90 days. As Trump put it, “This beef will be sold at 25 percent below current market prices.”

Americans consume roughly 7 million tons of ground beef in a year, or about 1.8 million tons over a given 90-day period. If we assume that none of the 300,000 tons would have been imported without the tariff relief, those additional supplies would add about 16.7 percent.

If we apply the demand elasticity estimates of consumer responses to changes in the price of ground beef as reported in the economic literature , the rough price reduction that we would expect from this temporary easing of tariffs would be no more than about 8 percent. Because some substantial portion of the 300,000 tons would have been imported in the absence of this Trump tariff reduction, the price effect will be smaller still.

So whence the Trump claim of a 25 percent price reduction? Surely he cannot believe that ground beef produced domestically will sell for so large a premium over the imported competitors. Or, as is so often the case, did Trump simply pull that number out of thin air?

Whatever the case, the temporary nature of the tariff reduction — it is no accident that the 90-day period ends not long after the midterm election — means that domestic producers will have incentives to put some of their ground beef in freezers in anticipation of increased prices after the 90-day period is over. Has Trump thought any of this through?

Remember when Trump claimed , repeatedly, that foreign producers would bear the costs of U.S. tariffs imposed upon imported goods? Because of the economic fundamentals shaping the international supplies of goods to the U.S., that claim was never realistic even remotely, and the economic literature is unambiguous that it is U.S. purchasers of imported goods who bear virtually the entire burden of tariffs.

Looming elections focus the minds of politicians, and Trump is no exception. His net approval poll numbers are underwater by roughly 30 points, and by about the same among all adults with respect to his tariff policies.

He cannot do much about gasoline prices — tariffs are not the source of recent increases — but he can deceive himself, and perhaps others, into believing that this tariff maneuver on ground beef will make an appreciable difference. When it fails to do so, it is a safe bet that he will again blame the private sector.

The cost of producing beef cattle has increased by 4.8 percent over the last year. The price of ground beef increased by 23 percent during former President Joe Biden’s first 18 months in office (39 percent during his four-year term), whereas the increase during Trump’s first 18 months is 24 percent.

Accordingly, Trump’s claim that “under Biden, beef prices soared at their fastest rate” is false, and whatever Trump may tell himself. Are his advisers simply incapable of telling him hard truths? And his own policies bear a substantial share of the blame.

Moreover, with respect to his complaint that “the American beef herd fell to its smallest size in modern history,” are the producers responsible for dry conditions and other problems? What does he think his effort to reduce prices will do to ameliorate that trend? And it is obvious that this tariff gambit might be repeated in the future; what effect will that have on the size of the herds?

Tariffs drive up production costs, as Trump now is conceding almost explicitly. The cost of cattle feed has increased 7.3 percent since Trump took office, in substantial part because fertilizer prices have increased, by around 50 percent globally since the beginning of the year. That this is the direct result of the Iran conflict and the partial closure of the Strait of Hormuz is obvious and acknowledged by the U.S. Farm Bureau, a prominent organization representing the agricultural sector and thus no fan of high input prices. Perhaps that is part of a price worth paying to confront the Iranian regime and its nuclear weapons program. But it is a price nonetheless.

Trump blames the previous administration for high beef prices. Trump blames the fossil energy producers for high gasoline prices because they are “ making too much money .” Trump blames vandalism for the problems with the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool even as it is clear that poor workmanship was a major cause. That Trump refuses to take responsibility for adverse outcomes is obvious. That he is incapable of doing so is obvious as well.

Benajmin Zycher is a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute.

articles.title: China-linked hackers infiltrated US government networks before FBI takedown
articles.summary: QTFY hackers breached three Energy Department labs and stole data from over 300 organizations before the FBI seized domains powering their platforms.
articles.body: Chinese state-linked hackers stole sensitive data from more than 300 organizations, including U.S. defense contractors, financial institutions and universities, and breached three Energy Department laboratories, the NIH and an HHS agency before the FBI knocked their hacking platforms offline this week, newly unsealed court records show. The group, known as QTFY, operated through a China-based company that the FBI says sold hacking services to clients including China’s Ministry of State Security and People’s Liberation Army. Former PLA members worked for the company and used military relationships to secure contracts and subcontracts for offensive cyber operations, according to an FBI affidavit. QTFY paired mass internet scanning with a network of compromised routers, cameras and other internet-connected devices that helped disguise the origin of its attacks. FBI SAYS RUSSIAN HACKERS HIJACKED OLD WI-FI ROUTERS By routing malicious traffic through devices near a victim’s network, the hackers could make attacks blend in with legitimate local traffic and become harder to trace, federal officials said. The Justice Department and FBI seized three domains Wednesday that powered QTFY’s two main platforms: QScan, which hunted for vulnerable systems, and QTRouter, which masked hackers’ identities by routing their traffic through compromised devices. Federal authorities said the seizures crippled both platforms by cutting off domains used for core communications and authentication. The scale was massive. AI IS NOW POWERING CYBERATTACKS, MICROSOFT WARNS On a single day in 2024, QScan processed more than 2 million scanning and penetration-testing tasks, according to the FBI affidavit. The platform contained more than 200 proof-of-concept exploits and searched the internet for vulnerable software, exposed services and other openings hackers could exploit. "QTFY is another example of how China’s cyber ecosystem has blurred the line between commercial cybersecurity and state-sponsored operations," Aaron Shraberg, senior intelligence team lead at Flashpoint, told Fox News Digital. "The commercialization of that ecosystem has helped turn capabilities that once relied on bespoke tradecraft into tools and services that can be developed, reused and deployed at scale." Federal authorities said QTFY targeted NASA, the Justice Department, the Federal Reserve and Senate systems, along with power companies, hospitals, telecommunications providers, defense contractors and election infrastructure. Fox News Digital has reached out to the Chinese embassy for comment. But not every attack worked. In 2019, QTFY tried to break into NASA using a vulnerability in the agency’s virtual private network. The attempt failed because NASA had already patched the flaw, according to the affidavit. A separate FBI, NSA and Cyber National Mission Force advisory said the group scanned Senate and hospital-system networks in March and a U.S. election system in June but failed to gain access. Other attacks succeeded. In May 2024, QTFY exploited a recently disclosed Check Point vulnerability while scanning U.S. power and telecommunications companies and stole data from more than 300 organizations in the United States and abroad, according to the advisory. The government did not name the affected organizations or describe what information was taken. The advisory said victims included U.S. defense contractors, financial institutions and universities. Four months later, hackers exploited zero-day flaws in Ivanti Cloud Services Appliance software to gain access to three Department of Energy national laboratories, the National Institutes of Health, the Health Resources and Services Administration and a U.S. security-device manufacturer, the advisory said. FBI BRINGS ALLEGED CHINA-LINKED HACKER TO US IN RARE EXTRADITION AS PATEL DEFENDS ITALY TRIP The advisory did not disclose what information was accessed, how long the hackers remained inside the networks or whether the breaches disrupted operations. "State-sponsored malicious hackers preying on America’s critical infrastructure will be stopped and prosecuted," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement announcing the seizures. The takedown adds to a string of FBI operations aimed at dismantling infrastructure used by Chinese government-linked hacking groups. In 2023, the FBI disrupted a botnet used by Volt Typhoon, a China-linked group accused of concealing its access to U.S. and foreign critical infrastructure. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER The following year, the bureau disabled a botnet made up of hundreds of thousands of infected internet-connected devices that federal officials said Flax Typhoon supplied to Chinese government customers. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Last year, the FBI said it removed PlugX surveillance malware from more than 4,000 U.S. computers infected by Mustang Panda, another China-linked hacking group.

articles.title: Maine Democrat backs Trump’s Canada tariffs: ‘It won’t go well for them’
articles.summary: Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine) doubled down on his support for President Trump’s tariff war with Canada, saying any retaliation stemming from the tariffs “won’t go well” for the neighboring country. “If Canada thinks they’re better off without our goods, I wish them good luck,” Golden told the Portland Press Herald on Tuesday. “I suspect in…
articles.body:
Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine) doubled down on his support for President Trump’s tariff war with Canada, saying any retaliation stemming from the tariffs “won’t go well” for the neighboring country.

“If Canada thinks they’re better off without our goods, I wish them good luck,” Golden told the Portland Press Herald on Tuesday. “I suspect in the long run, it won’t go well for them.”

The Trump administration introduced a 50 percent tariff on $20 billion worth of Canadian imports over the weekend after failed trade negotiations between the two nations. Trump also threatened 50 percent tariffs on vehicles and auto parts effective Jan. 1.

“America has been carrying Canada for decades, but no longer!” Trump wrote Monday on Truth Social . “Someone should get these clowns to ‘fall in line’ or, the consequences for Canada will be far WORSE!”

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on Wednesday said Canada sought concessions that were “too much” for the U.S. to agree to.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney responded with “dollar for dollar” retaliatory tariffs effective Sept. 8, targeting some of the Pine Tree State’s largest exports to Canada, including pulp and paper products and U.S.-harvested lobster.

Golden, who is not seeking reelection in Maine’s 2nd Congressional District reportedly due to threats against his family, has previously backed Trump’s tariff actions.

He was the lone House Democrat to vote against a resolution to repeal Trump’s tariffs on Canada, where six House Republicans joined Democrats in a 219-211 vote.

Some strategists have warned that the tariff war and its economic impact on Americans could cause problems for Republicans ahead of the midterms as the party scrambles to solidify its affordability messaging amid dwindling trust from voters.

“It really undermines our messaging when we’re trying to address affordability and we’re already having to deal with the price of oil due to the war in Iran,” Republican strategist Jason Cabel Roe told The Hill . “But that affordability debate only gets more complicated when we’re in a trade war with our largest trading partner, who happens to share a border with us.”

Other Maine politicians have pushed back on the tariffs over concerns about their trade impact. Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who is facing a competitive reelection race in November, called the latest tariffs “ a mistake ,” citing a “beneficial” trade relationship between the Republican’s home state and Canada.

State Auditor Matt Dunlap (D), who is looking to succeed Golden, used the tariffs as an opportunity to attack his opponent, former Maine Gov. Paul LePage (R), for having a “direct line” to the White House.

“Will Paul demand they end those tariff taxes that are hurting working families?” Dunlap said in a campaign video posted to social media . “Don’t hold your breath.”

articles.body: Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Thursday the indictments of 81 alleged members of Los Baja Deo, or LBD, a Puerto Rican-based drug trafficking organization. On Wednesday, the FBI and the Puerto Rico Police Department arrested 70 alleged LBD members on numerous charges. LBD has been active for years throughout the western side of the U.S. territory, Blanche said. The indictments charged the suspects with drug possession and distribution in connection to activities prosecutors said began in 2021. Blanche said 21 of the defendants were also charged with illegal firearms possession. They allegedly distributed "mass quantities" of cocaine, crack cocaine, fentanyl, heroin and marijuana, which generated $49 million in proceeds, Blanche said. WATCH: BLACK HAWK ASSISTS TAKEDOWN OF MASSIVE COCAINE HAUL OFF COAST OF PUERTO RICO Blanche said the defendants "maintained a steady supply of highly addictive and potentially lethal substances that endangered the community, fueled addiction and exposed entire public housing projects in Mayagüez and nearby neighborhoods to violence and chaos." The takedown of the 70 alleged LBD members took place following a San Juan Homeland Security Task Force investigation, according to the attorney general. Blanche called this "a great example of the success" Homeland Security has had in "combating violent crime and the illegal flow of narcotics." "If there's additional co-conspirators or members of this organization that have not been charged, I promise you that this investigation doesn't stop because an indictment is returned," Blanche said. "We'll find out. And if I were them, I would probably not be sleeping well tonight." NEVADA MAN FUNNELED 140 GUNS TO VIOLENT MEXICAN DRUG CARTELS, INCLUDING POWERFUL 'MILITARY-STYLE' RIFLES: DOJ Also announced at the press conference was an operation that took place Wednesday against Los Choneros and Los Lobos, Ecuador-based drug trafficking organizations. There were 26 arrests, including of four leaders of the Los Lobos cartel, Blanche said. This comes after local police arrested Eduardo Gomez, another alleged leader of the gang, at his home in Quito on May 14. Blanche said one metric ton of cocaine was seized from the two cartels, as well as around $1 million in U.S. currency. Additionally, authorities said they recovered 35 rifles, 26 vehicles, over 40 cellphones and an airplane. Three clandestine airports and landing strips were also destroyed. "President Trump called drug dealers terrorists, and that's because that's exactly what they are," Blanche said. "There are drug boats that are getting blown up because of trying to bring cocaine into our country." Blanche also announced the extradition of Erick Randhiel Mosquea Polanco, a long-sought cocaine kingpin from the Dominican Republic. He was transported from Colombia to San Juan to face charges in two separate cases. He also faces federal money laundering charges in New Jersey, Blanche said.

articles.title: Democrats hand Trump one power they spent years fighting
articles.summary: Senate Democrats voted to give Trump limited tariff authority in exchange for Russia sanctions, a move some warn he could exploit against trade partners.
articles.body: After raging against a key tool in President Donald Trump’s economic arsenal, Senate Democrats quietly green-lit the authority before they left Washington, D.C. Democrats have bashed Trump’s use of tariffs since they were first floated during his campaign in 2024, and have taken every chance to challenge and push back against duties imposed on other countries throughout his second term. But nearly the entire Senate Democratic caucus voted in favor of giving Trump limited tariff authority in exchange for bone-crushing sanctions against Russia. Only nine Democrats, and Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., ultimately voted against the package. PUTIN, RUSSIA PUT ON NOTICE AS SENATE TAKES CRUCIAL STEP TO GRIND DOWN THE KREMLIN’S WAR MACHINE Now, Trump has ignited a trade war with Canada, introducing 50% tariffs against the country on roughly $20 billion worth of goods, which has reignited the debate on the campaign trail and as Democrats seek to flip the Senate and corral his authority. Some warned that giving congressional approval would allow the administration to abuse the power. "It gives Donald Trump massive new tariff authority that he can use to threaten our trading partners and raise prices on the American people," Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., said on the Senate floor. "I believe senators will come to deeply regret voting to give Donald Trump this tariff authority." Though not directly connected to the authority granted in the sanctions package, which directly deals with countries buying oil from Russia, Trump’s move to enter into a fight with one of America’s top trade partners is what he warned of: giving the White House congressional leeway. TRUMP ALLIES PUSH TO ARM PRESIDENT WITH NEW TARIFF WEAPON TO PUNISH COUNTRIES 'RIPPING OFF' AMERICA The tariff authority baked into the sanctions package would allow Trump to issue levies of up to 500% on Russian imports and tariffs of up to 100% on the top five countries buying Russian energy, like China and India. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., who, alongside the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, pushed the package for nearly two years, told Fox News Digital that if Trump strays outside the legal confines built into the package, the courts will block him as they did with his sweeping tariffs unveiled on "Liberation Day" last year. "If Donald Trump wants to break this law, he will be restrained by the courts, just as when he broke the law on tariffs previously," Blumenthal said. "We can't do any more than be explicit in limiting his authority to the top five purchasers, and only those countries, by the terms, specific in the legislation." Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who went on to vote against the package, told reporters last month that Trump "has shown what he will do with broad tariff authority." TRUMP BET TARIFFS WOULD BRING BACK AMERICAN FACTORY JOBS. NEW REPORT SAYS IT DIDN'T WORK "Heck, he’s shown what he’ll do even if he doesn’t have authority," she said. And Paul, who has been one of the lone Republicans to consistently oppose Trump's use of tariffs, introduced an amendment alongside Wyden to strip them from the broader package, warning that the duties were nothing more than an additional tax on the American people. "Do not let sympathy for Ukraine blind you to the reality of tariffs," Paul said. One Senate Democrat, Sen. Raphael Warnock, D-Ga., received guarantees from U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer that the tariffs baked into the sanctions package would just be limited to the top five energy trading partners with the Kremlin. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He told Fox News Digital that the concern was that Trump could broadly bend the rules in the package and impose duties as he pleased, which is why he sought guardrails and commitments from the administration. "It was important to hold [Vladimir] Putin accountable. He is a war criminal," Warnock said. "His aggression towards Ukraine has national security implications for us. But at the same time, it was important to put some guardrails on this president. And I think I made considerable progress in making sure that that happens."

articles.title: DHS fires 3 more FEMA workers after IG report finds crew skipped homes with pro-Trump signs
articles.summary: DHS fired three more FEMA workers after an inspector general report found crews skipped homes with Trump signs during Hurricane Milton relief.
articles.body: The Department of Homeland Security fired three more FEMA workers on Thursday after an inspector general report found that FEMA crews skipped servicing homes with pro-Trump signs following Hurricane Milton. DHS says the three firings were in addition to other firings carried out after the IG report released last week. An investigation by FEMA's Office of Professional Responsibility found that the three employees had "failed to meet FEMA's standards of conduct." "Our job is to protect the American people, regardless of their political beliefs. This is especially important when it comes to disaster relief, where every second counts and lives are on the line," said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. "We’ve made sure that everyone responsible for this incident has been punished, and we’ll make sure that nothing like this ever happens again." DEM GOV LASHES OUT AS TRUMP HUD SCRUTINIZES NEARLY $2B IN DISASTER FUNDS OVER FRAUD CONCERNS "Thanks to President Trump, FEMA has been empowered to hold accountable those who are responsible and has changed how it conducts survivor outreach to ensure Americans are treated fairly and assistance is driven by need," said FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton. "Under my watch, all parties involved in this situation have been held accountable. Political bias has no room in public service," he added. The firings come after FEMA supervisor Marn’i Washington was fired for instructing personnel to avoid homes with Trump signage in Lake Placid, Florida, in 2024. Washington maintains she did nothing wrong, arguing in statements to the Washington Post that she was looking to protect workers in a highly politicized environment. NORTH CAROLINA MOUNTAIN COMMUNITY BRACES FOR HURRICANE SEASON TWO YEARS AFTER HELENE'S BRUTAL IMPACT "I had never seen people so passionate during that political season, and what we were experiencing was not just conspiracy theories. People were physically charging at us with aggressive postures and accusations," Washington told the Post. "People calling people on the phone saying FEMA was here. They would beat us to the fence and yell: ‘Don’t come here, you are part of Biden; we know what Biden is doing. You are taking our money and giving it to immigrants.’ ‘Drain the swamp’ was a common term," she said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Washington claimed that her teams only avoided homes that showed both a Trump sign and further signs of so-called hostility, such as signs referencing guns.

Greg Abbott (R) is leading Democrat Gina Hinojosa in the gubernatorial race in the Lone Star State, according to a new poll from Texas Public Opinion Research. In the poll, 47 percent of respondents said they would back Talarico…
articles.body:
Democrat James Talarico is leading Republican Ken Paxton in the Senate race in Texas, while Gov. Greg Abbott (R) is leading Democrat Gina Hinojosa in the gubernatorial race in the Lone Star State, according to a new poll from Texas Public Opinion Research .

In the poll , 47 percent of respondents said they would back Talarico if the election occurred that day, while 40 percent went for Paxton. Another 1 percent backed a Libertarian candidate, 11 percent were undecided and 1 percent rejected the idea of voting.

The poll also found Hinojosa 7 points behind Abbott among respondents who were asked which candidate they’d vote for if the election occurred that day, with the Democrat at 41 percent support to the Republican’s 48 percent. A Libertarian candidate garnered 1 percent support, while 8 percent of respondents were undecided and 1 percent rejected the idea of voting.

The two showdowns in the Lone Star State come as Democrats look to make key gains in the midterms amid rocky political territory for the GOP. Democrats have sought in recent years to notch electoral wins in Texas but haven’t had much success , as seen in races such as former Rep. Beto O’Rourke’s (D) challenge to Sen. Ted Cruz (R) in 2018.

Abbott is looking to secure a fourth term leading his state, which hasn’t elected a Democratic governor in more than a quarter of a century , so an upset by Hinojosa would be significant.

While Democrats usually have an uphill battle in the Lone Star State, Paxton comes with notable baggage. The Texas attorney general has been dogged by scandal, previously facing impeachment in the Texas House on corruption charges before being acquitted in the Texas Senate.

A few weeks ago, Talarico’s campaign confirmed it poached a former staffer for Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), whom Talarico and Paxton are racing to replace in November, to join the Democratic candidate on the campaign trail.

The Texas Public Opinion Research poll took place from Aug. 21 to 26, featuring 1,000 likely voters in Texas and a margin of error of 3.3 percentage points.

Beside Trump…
articles.body:
President Trump signed an executive order Thursday formally changing the name of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” amid the U.S. trade war with Canada.

“We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario effective immediately to Lake America,” Trump told reporters before he signed an executive order renaming the body of water.

Beside Trump in the Oval Office, placards of the Great Lakes were displayed, with “Lake America” named over Lake Ontario.

“We filed all of the necessary papers, documents, [and] everything else. We’ve notified all of the various people you have to notify,” the president said.

The executive order comes after Trump first publicly floated changing the name of the easternmost Great Lake earlier this week as the trade war picked up between Washington and Ottawa.

The president told reporters he had been thinking about renaming Lake Ontario for “a long time.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded earlier this week to the president’s initial threats to rename the lake, calling it “a lot of rhetoric.”

This is not the first time Trump has renamed a body of water bordering the U.S. and another country. Last year, Trump signed an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America.”

“If you think about it, we have a gulf, now we have a lake, now all we need is an ocean,” Trump quipped. Maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them both.”

Trade tensions between Washington and Ottawa devolved into an all-out trade war over the weekend after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney removed negotiators from trade talks with the U.S.

Carney’s move came before a new set of tariffs from the Trump administration on Canada were set to go into effect.

The prime minister then announced Ottawa would enact retaliatory tariffs in response to the U.S.’s new 50 percent tariffs starting Sept. 8. The Canadian leader said during a press conference that his nation would “match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families and businesses.”

articles.body:
President Trump signed an executive order Thursday afternoon that renames Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” following through on an idea he floated as the U.S.-Canada trade war hit fever pitch in recent days.

Trump’s battle to make the Kennedy Center his own returns to court Thursday, where a judge will hear arguments about whether Trump’s name may be inscribed on the building.

Earlier this week, the Justice Department argued in court filings that the renowned performing arts facility will suffer financial ruin if his name isn’t attached and may need to be demolished if it doesn’t receive renovations — for which Trump would also like recognition. A hearing related to the case is set for 2 p.m. EDT.

In Texas, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer accused of shooting a Venezuelan man in the leg during an immigration crackdown in Minnesota earlier this year was released from jail Thursday morning. A day earlier, a judge declined to force his extradition to Minnesota. Christian Castro was freed from custody just before 7 a.m. local time, Cameron County Sheriff Manuel Treviño confirmed in an email to The Hill.

The president will head Thursday to Texas to headline a fundraiser for the Republican National Committee that aims to boost the chances of Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general.

The Texas Senate race is considered a toss-up by election watchers, with Democrat James Talarico and Paxton running neck and neck in recent polls.

Before leaving for the Lone Star State, the president has a policy meeting and signing time on his schedule.
